solution: [For any $f:X->Y$, both $(f times f)"swap"_X$ and $"swap"_Y(f times f)$ send $(x,y)$ to $(f(y),f(x))$, proving naturality. Each swap composed with itself is the identity, so each component is invertible; the inverse family is the same natural transformation. Thus it is a natural isomorphism.]
criteria: [Check naturality and invertibility independently.]

question: [Construct the pullback in sets of two maps to a singleton and prove its universal property.]
hint1: [Compatibility is automatic.]
hint2: [The construction is a Cartesian product.]
solution: [For $A -> 1$ and $B -> 1$, every pair $(a,b)$ is compatible, so the pullback is $A times B$. Given maps from $X$ to $A,B$, the unique mediator is their pairing. Both composites to the singleton agree automatically, so this is exactly the pullback property.]
criteria: [Explain why there is no remaining compatibility restriction.]

question: [Classify natural transformations $X^3 -> X^2$ in sets and count them.]
hint1: [Represent the two powers by finite sets.]
hint2: [They correspond to functions from a two-element set to a three-element set.]
solution: [Yoneda gives $"Nat"("Set"(3,-),"Set"(2,-)) iso "Set"(2,3)$. Each of the two output coordinates independently selects one of the three input coordinates. There are $3^2=9$ transformations, explicitly $(x_1,x_2,x_3)|->(x_i,x_j)$ for $i,j in\{1,2,3\}$.]
criteria: [Justify exhaustiveness with Yoneda.]

question: [Prove a left adjoint preserves initial objects directly from its hom-set bijection.]
hint1: [Count maps from the image of an initial object.]
hint2: [The corresponding source hom set is a singleton.]
solution: [If $I$ is initial in $cal(C)$ and $F tack.l G$, then for every $D$ the adjunction gives $cal(D)(F I,D) iso cal(C)(I,G D)$. The right set has exactly one element, so the left does too. This is precisely initiality of $F I$.]
criteria: [Use all targets $D$, not one particular object.]

question: [Prove every functor preserves isomorphisms.]
hint1: [Apply it to both inverse equations.]
hint2: [The image of an inverse is an inverse.]
solution: [If $g f=1$ and $f g=1$, then functoriality gives $F g F f=F(g f)=1$ and $F f F g=F(f g)=1$. Thus $F f$ is an isomorphism with inverse $F g$.]
criteria: [Use identity preservation as well as composition preservation.]

question: [For free vector spaces, describe the unit at a set $X$ and counit at a vector space $V$.]
hint1: [Distinguish generators from formal sums of actual vectors.]
hint2: [Insertion and evaluation are the two maps.]
solution: [The unit sends $x$ to its basis vector $[x]$ in the underlying set of $F X$. The counit sends $sum_i a_i[v_i]$ in $F U V$ to the actual vector sum $sum_i a_i v_i$ in $V$.]
criteria: [Give the source and target of each map.]

question: [Compute the coequalizer in vector spaces of $f,g:K -> K^2$ given by $f(t)=(t,0)$ and $g(t)=(0,t)$.]
hint1: [Quotient by the image of $f-g$.]
hint2: [The map $(a,b)|->a+b$ has the required kernel.]
solution: [The image of $f-g$ is the line spanned by $(1,-1)$. The quotient is one-dimensional and is identified with $K$ by $(a,b)|->a+b$, whose kernel is that line and which is surjective. This map coequalizes $f,g$ and has the quotient universal property.]
criteria: [The formula also works in characteristic two.]

question: [Show the functor $G |-> G times G$ from groups to sets is represented by a free group on two generators.]
hint1: [A homomorphism from a free group is determined by generator images.]
hint2: [Any ordered pair of group elements is permitted.]
solution: [Let $F_2$ be free on $a,b$. Sending a homomorphism to $(f(a),f(b))$ is bijective by the free-group property. Postcomposition applies a group homomorphism to both entries, so this bijection is natural. Hence the underlying-pair functor is represented by $F_2$.]
criteria: [Use the free-group universal property, not the direct product of two copies of $ZZ$.]

question: [Let $F$ be full, faithful, and essentially surjective. Prove it sends a terminal object to a terminal object.]
hint1: [Represent an arbitrary target-category object up to isomorphism by $F A$.]
hint2: [Use the hom-set bijection supplied by full faithfulness.]
solution: [For any target object $D$, choose an isomorphism $F A -> D$. Maps $D -> F T$ correspond by precomposition to maps $F A -> F T$, and full faithfulness identifies the latter with maps $A -> T$. Since $T$ is terminal, this set is a singleton. Thus every $D$ has exactly one map to $F T$, proving terminality.]
criteria: [Explain why essential surjectivity is needed to cover every $D$.]

question: [In the power-set poset of $S$, identify a right adjoint to intersection with a fixed $A$ and derive its counit inequality.]
hint1: [Solve $X inter A subset.eq B$ for the largest permissible $X$.]
hint2: [The largest choice is $(S without A) union B$.]
solution: [The right adjoint is $G(B)=(S without A) union B$, since $X inter A subset.eq B$ iff $X subset.eq G(B)$. Its counit is $G(B) inter A subset.eq B$, which holds because an element in $A$ cannot be in its complement and must therefore belong to $B$.]
criteria: [State the adjunction equivalence and derive the correctly oriented inequality.]

question: [Verify that nonnegative integers with an arrow $m -> n$ exactly when $m<=n$ form a category.]
hint1: [Use reflexivity and transitivity.]
hint2: [There is at most one arrow of each type.]
solution: [Reflexivity supplies identities; transitivity supplies a composite whenever arrows are composable. Both possible associative composites have the same source and target and hence are the unique arrow of that type. Identity laws hold for the same reason.]
criteria: [Check identities, existence of composition, and associativity.]

question: [Describe the one-object category associated with the additive monoid $NN$. What arrows are invertible?]
hint1: [Composition is addition and identity is zero.]
hint2: [An inverse would be a nonnegative integer adding to zero.]
solution: [There is one object, arrows are nonnegative integers, composition is addition, and the identity arrow is zero. Only zero is invertible, since $n+m=0$ with both nonnegative forces both zero.]
criteria: [Distinguish the object from its many endomorphisms.]

question: [Describe the opposite of a poset category.]
hint1: [Reverse the order relation.]
hint2: [An arrow $a -> b$ now means $b<=a$.]
solution: [The opposite has the same objects with the reversed order. Identities are unchanged, and transitivity of the reversed order supplies composition.]
criteria: [State the new arrow condition explicitly.]

question: [Prove an isomorphism in the category of groups is exactly a bijective group homomorphism.]
hint1: [The inverse of a bijection must also preserve the operation.]
hint2: [Apply the original homomorphism to the desired inverse equation.]
solution: [An inverse morphism makes the underlying function bijective. Conversely let $f:G -> H$ be a bijective homomorphism. For $x=f(a),y=f(b)$, $f^(-1)(x y)=f^(-1)(f(a b))=a b=f^(-1)(x)f^(-1)(y)$. Thus its inverse function is a homomorphism.]
criteria: [Prove the reverse direction rather than treating inverse preservation as automatic.]

question: [Prove the composite of two monomorphisms is monic.]
hint1: [Cancel one factor at a time.]
hint2: [From $n m u=n m v$, first cancel $n$.]
solution: [If $n,m$ are monic and $(n m)u=(n m)v$, monicity of $n$ gives $m u=m v$, then monicity of $m$ gives $u=v$. This is the definition of monicity of the composite.]
criteria: [State the sources and targets needed for all composites.]

question: [If $g f$ is monic, prove $f$ is monic. Must $g$ be monic?]
hint1: [Precompose both sides of an equality with $g$.]
hint2: [For the counterexample use an inclusion followed by a constant map on a larger set.]
solution: [If $f u=f v$, then $g f u=g f v$, so monicity of $g f$ gives $u=v$. The second claim fails: let $f$ include a singleton into a two-element set and let $g$ be the constant map to a singleton. The composite is a bijection on a singleton, hence monic, but $g$ is not injective.]
criteria: [Prove the implication and supply a fully typed counterexample.]

question: [Show a morphism with a left inverse is monic. Give a monomorphism of sets with no left inverse.]
hint1: [Use cancellation for the proof; consider the empty set for the example.]
hint2: [The map from the empty set to a singleton is injective.]
solution: [If $r f=1$, then $f u=f v$ implies $u=r f u=r f v=v$. The unique map $emptyset -> 1$ is injective and therefore monic, but it has no left inverse because no map $1 -> emptyset$ exists.]
criteria: [A left inverse must be an actual arrow with the required source.]

question: [Prove a function missing an element of its codomain is not epic in sets.]
hint1: [Construct two functions from the codomain to a two-element set.]
hint2: [Make them differ only at the missing element.]
solution: [If $f:X -> Y$ misses $y_0$, let $u:Y -> \{0,1\}$ be constantly zero and let $v$ be one at $y_0$ and zero elsewhere. Then $u!=v$ but $u f=v f$, because $f$ never reaches $y_0$. Hence $f$ fails the epi cancellation property.]
criteria: [Specify the test maps and why their composites agree.]

question: [Show the isomorphisms in any category, retaining all objects, form a subcategory in which every arrow is invertible.]
hint1: [Check identities and composition.]
hint2: [The inverse of $g f$ is $f^(-1)g^(-1)$.]
solution: [Identities are isomorphisms. For isomorphisms $f:A->B$ and $g:B->C$, the composite $g f$ has proposed inverse $f^(-1)g^(-1)$. It satisfies both inverse equations by associativity, so composites of isomorphisms remain isomorphisms. The inverses themselves are isomorphisms, hence lie in this subcategory. It is a groupoid.]
criteria: [Verify the composition order.]

question: [Prove a morphism that is both monic and split epic is an isomorphism.]
hint1: [Let $f s=1$.]
hint2: [Compare $f(s f)$ with $f$.]
solution: [Let $f:A->B$ and choose its right inverse $s:B->A$. Since $f s=1_B$, we have $f(s f)=(f s)f=f=f 1_A$. Monicity of $f$ gives $s f=1_A$. Thus $s$ is both a right and left inverse, and $f$ is an isomorphism.]
criteria: [Do not assume an arbitrary epi has a section.]

question: [Prove the inclusion $ZZ -> ZZ[1/2]$ is epic among commutative unital rings but is not an isomorphism.]
hint1: [A map must send $1/2$ to the inverse of two.]
hint2: [Inverses, when they exist, are unique.]
solution: [If two homomorphisms out of $ZZ[1/2]$ agree on $ZZ$, their values on $1/2$ are both inverses of the common image of two, hence agree. Every element is $a/2^n$, so all their values agree. This proves the inclusion epic. It is not onto because $1/2$ is not an integer, and a ring isomorphism must be a bijection.]
criteria: [Quantify over every possible target ring and compare all fractions.]

question: [Construct the free category on a directed graph and prove any assignment of its vertices and edges to objects and arrows of a category extends uniquely to a functor.]
hint1: [Use finite composable paths, including empty paths.]
hint2: [A functor must send a path to the composite of its edge images.]
solution:
[*Finding the approach.* The graph has generators but no composites yet. Build the missing arrows formally, so that no accidental equation is imposed beyond the category axioms.

*Argument.* Objects are vertices; arrows are finite composable paths; empty paths are identities; composition concatenates paths. Concatenation is associative. Given a graph assignment preserving endpoints, send each path to the composite of its edge images and each empty path to an identity. Associativity and identity laws in the target prove this is a functor. Every path is a composite of edges, so any extension must have these values, proving uniqueness.

A path has specified initial and terminal vertices; only matching endpoints may be concatenated. Parenthesizing concatenations does not change the edge sequence. For an image of a length-three path, the two possible target composites agree by associativity, and induction handles every finite length. Empty paths must map to identities, so the construction also covers isolated vertices. Uniqueness is equality on all paths, not just on the graph's edges.

*A tempting dead end.* Do not identify different paths merely because they have the same endpoints. That produces a thin category and destroys the freedom to map parallel paths to different arrows.

*Hypotheses.* The graph assignment must preserve endpoints. The target's associativity and identity laws are what make evaluation of formal paths a functor.]
criteria: [Include empty paths and explain why no additional path relations are imposed.]
idea: [Keep paths formal until evaluating them in the target; the functor axioms then force every value.]

question: [Form a category with one object whose arrows are finite words in the two symbols $a,b$, including the empty word; composition is concatenation. Verify the category laws, determine which arrows are monomorphisms and epimorphisms, and determine which are isomorphisms.]
hint1: [Equality of words records every letter and its position.]
hint2: [Concatenation has cancellation on either side; lengths add.]
solution:
[*Finding the approach.* In a one-object category, cancellation definitions are equations between words. Length gives an independent obstruction to invertibility.

*Argument.* Associativity holds because concatenating three words produces the same ordered sequence under either parenthesization. The empty word is a two-sided identity. If $w u=w v$, delete the identical initial segment $w$ to obtain $u=v$; if $u w=v w$, compare lengths first and then delete the identical final segment to obtain $u=v$. Thus every arrow is both monic and epic, regardless of the chosen convention for which factor is applied first. If $w$ has an inverse $v$, their concatenation is empty and $|w|+|v|=0$. Both lengths are nonnegative, so $w$ is empty. Conversely the empty word is its own inverse. In particular a nonempty word is monic and epic without being an isomorphism.

*A tempting dead end.* The implication 'monic and epic means invertible' is true in sets but not in every category. This category provides the missing counterexample.

*Hypotheses.* Arrows are words themselves, not words modulo additional relations. Quotienting by relations can destroy cancellation or introduce inverses.]
criteria: [Check both cancellation directions and distinguish them from existence of an inverse.]
idea: [Use cancellation to analyze mono and epi, then a different invariant—length—to analyze inverses.]

question: [Show a monotone map between posets gives a functor between their categories.]
hint1: [The object map is the given function.]
hint2: [Monotonicity supplies the required arrow images.]
solution: [If $a<=b$, monotonicity gives $F(a)<=F(b)$, so the unique arrow maps to the unique arrow. Identities and composites are preserved because the relevant hom sets contain at most one arrow.]
criteria: [Explain why monotonicity is exactly the condition needed.]

question: [Define the forgetful functor from vector spaces over $K$ to sets on objects and arrows.]
hint1: [Retain the underlying data.]
hint2: [Linear maps are functions.]
solution: [It sends a vector space to its underlying set and a linear map to its underlying function. Identity linear maps are identity functions and linear-map composition is function composition, proving the functor laws.]
criteria: [Describe both assignments.]

question: [For $f:X -> Y$, write the map $cal(C)(A,f)$.]
hint1: [Postcompose an arrow from $A$.]
hint2: [Its input is $h:A -> X$.]
solution: [It is the function $cal(C)(A,X) -> cal(C)(A,Y)$, $h |-> f h$. The types ensure the composite exists.]
criteria: [Give domain, codomain, and formula.]

question: [Explain why the forgetful functor from groups to sets is faithful.]
hint1: [Compare two homomorphisms with the same underlying function.]
hint2: [Morphisms are actual functions with a property.]
solution: [If two group homomorphisms have equal underlying functions, they take the same value at every group element and are the same homomorphism. Thus each induced hom-set map is injective.]
criteria: [Use the hom-set definition of faithful.]

question: [Verify inverse image of subsets is a contravariant functor on sets.]
hint1: [Test identity and a composite.]
hint2: [An element belongs to an inverse image exactly when its image belongs to the target subset.]
solution: [For $f:X -> Y,g:Y -> Z$ and $S subset.eq Z$, $x in (g f)^(-1)S$ exactly when $g(f(x)) in S$, equivalently $x in f^(-1)(g^(-1)S)$. Thus composition reverses. Identity inverse image is the identity on the power set.]
criteria: [State the reversed direction of the arrow map.]

question: [Show the forgetful functor from groups to sets is not full.]
hint1: [Find a function which does not preserve the identity.]
hint2: [Use a constant nonidentity value in a nontrivial group.]
solution: [The constant function $C_2 -> C_2$ with value its nonidentity element is a set function but cannot be a group homomorphism, since homomorphisms send identity to identity. Therefore the hom-set map is not surjective.]
criteria: [Use a map between underlying sets of actual objects in the source category.]

question: [Prove a full and faithful functor reflects isomorphisms.]
hint1: [Lift the inverse of $F f$ using fullness.]
hint2: [Use faithfulness on the two inverse equations.]
solution: [If $F f$ has inverse $u$, fullness gives $g$ with $F g=u$. Then $F(g f)=F g F f=1=F(1)$ and similarly $F(f g)=F(1)$. Faithfulness gives $g f=1$ and $f g=1$, so $f$ is an isomorphism.]
criteria: [Specify which property supplies the inverse candidate and which verifies its equations.]

question: [Show functors between one-object categories of monoids are precisely monoid homomorphisms.]
hint1: [Only the arrow assignment is variable.]
hint2: [Identity and composition become unit and multiplication.]
solution: [The unique object must map to the unique object. The arrow map is a function between monoids. The two functor laws require it to preserve the unit and multiplication, exactly the monoid-homomorphism axioms. Conversely those axioms define a functor.]
criteria: [State both directions of the identification.]

question: [Show the category of matrices over $K$, with objects nonnegative integers, is equivalent to finite-dimensional vector spaces.]
hint1: [Map $n$ to $K^n$.]
hint2: [Every linear map between coordinate spaces has a unique matrix.]
solution: [The matrix-to-linear-map functor preserves multiplication and identities. The uniqueness and existence of coordinate matrices make it full and faithful. Every finite-dimensional vector space has a finite basis and is isomorphic to some $K^n$, giving essential surjectivity. The equivalence criterion applies.]
criteria: [Include dimension zero and distinguish essential from literal surjectivity.]

question: [Prove a faithful functor reflects monomorphisms and epimorphisms, without assuming fullness.]
hint1: [Apply the functor to the relevant equality.]
hint2: [Cancel in the target, then use faithfulness.]
solution: [If $F f$ is monic and $f u=f v$, then $F f F u=F f F v$, so $F u=F v$ and faithfulness gives $u=v$. Thus $f$ is monic. Dually, if $F f$ is epic and $u f=v f$, cancel $F f$ on the right and use faithfulness to conclude $u=v$.]
criteria: [Do not confuse reflection with preservation; fullness is unnecessary here.]

question: [Show equivalent poset categories are isomorphic as posets.]
hint1: [Natural isomorphisms between objects in a poset are equalities.]
hint2: [A quasi-inverse is actually inverse on objects.]
solution: [If $F,G$ witness an equivalence, the component isomorphisms $G F(p) iso p$ and $F G(q) iso q$ force literal equality by antisymmetry. Thus the monotone maps are inverse bijections. Each direction is monotone, so they are an order isomorphism.]
criteria: [Use antisymmetry; the statement need not hold for preorders.]

question: [Construct a faithful functor which sends a monomorphism and epimorphism to a function which is neither. Use the two-object poset $0<1$ as source, and explain why this does not contradict #link(label("MM7030-U2.10"))[U2.10].]
hint1: [Every arrow in a poset category is monic and epic.]
hint2: [Send the sole nonidentity arrow to a constant map between two-element sets.]
solution:
[*Finding the approach.* Faithfulness only compares arrows already present in each source hom set. A thin source makes that requirement easy to satisfy even when its target has many more test arrows.

*Argument.* Map both objects to the set $\{a,b\}$, identities to identities, and $0->1$ to the constant function with value $a$. These assignments form a functor because every nontrivial composition involves an identity. It is faithful: each source hom set is empty or a singleton, so its map into the corresponding function set is injective. The nonidentity source arrow is both monic and epic, but its image is neither injective nor surjective, hence neither monic nor epic in sets. Faithfulness reflects cancellation properties from the target; it does not preserve them from the source.

To see failure of monicity in sets, choose the two distinct functions from a singleton selecting $a$ and $b$; composing either with the constant map gives the same function. To see failure of epicity, choose two functions from the two-point codomain to itself that agree at $a$ but differ at $b$. Their composites with the constant map agree. These witnesses are absent from the relevant source hom sets, so faithfulness cannot rule them out.

*A tempting dead end.* A faithful functor need not be full, injective on objects, or preserve every categorical property. The direction of a reflection argument cannot be reversed.

*Hypotheses.* The source is a poset viewed as a category, so every parallel pair there is equal. Cancellation in the target must be tested against all target arrows, not only image arrows.]
criteria: [Verify functoriality and faithfulness, and distinguish preservation from reflection.]
idea: [Identify the missing target test arrows to understand exactly why reflection does not imply preservation.]

question: [Let objects be pairs $(X,e)$ with $X$ a finite set and $e:X -> X$ satisfying $e^2=e$. An arrow $f:(X,e) -> (Y,d)$ satisfies $f e=f=d f$, and the identity of $(X,e)$ is $e$. Verify this is a category. Show that sending $(X,e)$ to its image $e(X)$ and arrows to restrictions gives an equivalence with finite sets.]
hint1: [Each point of the image of an idempotent is fixed by that idempotent.]
hint2: [Extend a function $h:e(X) -> d(Y)$ to $X$ by $x |-> h(e(x))$.]
solution:
[*Finding the approach.* The unusual identity tells us that points outside the image carry no independent information. Restriction should remove exactly that redundancy, and the displayed extension tests whether any information is lost.

*Argument.* Compositions satisfy the same equations: if $f e=f=d f$ and $g d=g=c g$, then $(g f)e=g f$ and $c(g f)=g f$. Composition is associative as composition of functions, and $e,d$ act as the required identities on $f$. Every $f$ maps into $d(Y)$ and is determined by its restriction to $e(X)$ because $f(x)=f(e(x))$. Conversely any function $h:e(X) -> d(Y)$ extends to $f(x)=h(e(x))$; idempotence gives both arrow equations. Restriction is therefore a bijection on each hom set, hence full and faithful. Every finite set $Z$ is the image of $(Z,id_Z)$, so the functor is essentially surjective and an equivalence. The inclusion and retraction between $(X,e)$ and $(e(X),id)$ have composites $e$ and the identity, exactly the identities in this category.

*A tempting dead end.* The identity on the underlying set $X$ is generally not an arrow of this category. Using it in place of $e$ breaks the verification.

*Hypotheses.* Idempotence is essential both for the category's identities and for the extension formula. Finiteness keeps the target within the chosen category but is not used in the hom-set bijection.]
criteria: [Verify the category first, then prove fullness, faithfulness, and essential surjectivity explicitly.]
idea: [Restriction and extension are inverse descriptions of arrows, while every target object already occurs as an image.]

question: [Write the naturality equation for $eta:F => G$ at $f:A -> B$.]
hint1: [Draw a square with $F A,G A,F B,G B$.]
hint2: [Both paths must run from $F A$ to $G B$.]
solution: [The equation is $G(f)eta_A=eta_B F(f)$. The left path goes first across at $A$ and then down by $G f$; the right path first uses $F f$ and then the component at $B$.]
criteria: [Check the domain and codomain of each factor.]

question: [Show the identity maps $1_(F A)$ form a natural transformation $F => F$.]
hint1: [Insert them into the naturality equation.]
hint2: [Both sides reduce to $F f$.]
solution: [$F f 1_(F A)=F f=1_(F B)F f$ by identity laws. Thus the component family is natural.]
criteria: [Use identity arrows at the correct objects.]

question: [Show $pi_1:X times X -> X$ is natural in the set $X$.]
hint1: [The product functor sends $f$ to $f times f$.]
hint2: [Evaluate both composites on $(x,y)$.]
solution: [Both $f pi_1$ and $pi_1(f times f)$ send $(x,y)$ to $f(x)$. Hence the square commutes for every function $f$, proving naturality.]
criteria: [Quantify over all functions.]

question: [Describe a natural transformation between two constant functors with values $A,B$ when the source is the terminal one-object category.]
hint1: [There is just one component.]
hint2: [The only naturality equation involves identity arrows.]
solution: [It is any arrow $A -> B$. The sole naturality equation is $1_B eta=eta 1_A$, automatically true.]
criteria: [Explain why no additional compatibility condition occurs.]

question: [Show the diagonal $Delta_X:X -> X times X$ is natural and each component is injective.]
hint1: [Evaluate on an element.]
hint2: [Both square paths produce $(f(x),f(x))$.]
solution: [For any $f:X -> Y$, $(f times f)Delta_X(x)=(f(x),f(x))=Delta_Y f(x)$, proving naturality. If $Delta_X(x)=Delta_X(y)$, equality of first coordinates gives $x=y$, so each component is injective.]
criteria: [Prove naturality separately from injectivity.]

question: [Prove vertical composition of natural transformations is associative.]
hint1: [Compute the component at an arbitrary object.]
hint2: [Use associativity in the target category.]
solution: [For composable $eta,theta,kappa$, the components of $(kappa theta)eta$ and $kappa(theta eta)$ are $(kappa_A theta_A)eta_A$ and $kappa_A(theta_A eta_A)$, equal by associativity. Transformations are equal when all components agree, so composition is associative.]
criteria: [Include the componentwise equality criterion.]

question: [If $eta:F => G$ is natural and each component is invertible, prove the inverse family is natural.]
hint1: [Rearrange the naturality equation by composing with inverses.]
hint2: [Start from $G f eta_A=eta_B F f$.]
solution: [Compose on the left with $eta_B^(-1)$ and on the right with $eta_A^(-1)$ to obtain $eta_B^(-1)G f=F f eta_A^(-1)$. This is the naturality equation for a transformation $G => F$. Componentwise inverse equations make it the inverse transformation.]
criteria: [Keep the indices consistent.]

question: [For two actions of a group $G$ on sets $X,Y$, show natural transformations of the corresponding functors are exactly equivariant functions.]
hint1: [There is one component, a function $T:X -> Y$.]
hint2: [Naturality at $g$ is the equivariance equation.]
solution: [Because the group category has one object, the component family is one function $T$. Naturality at each arrow $g$ says $T(g dot x)=g dot T(x)$ for every $x$. These are precisely the equations defining an equivariant function. Conversely an equivariant function satisfies every naturality square.]
criteria: [State both directions.]

question: [Verify naturality of the canonical map $V -> V^(**)$ by evaluating on a linear functional.]
hint1: [Equality of functionals can be checked at an arbitrary argument.]
hint2: [For $f:V -> W$ and $psi in W^*$, both values are $psi(f(v))$.]
solution: [Let $eta_V(v)(phi)=phi(v)$. Then $f^(**)(eta_V(v))(psi)=eta_V(v)(psi f)=psi(f(v))=eta_W(f(v))(psi)$. Equality for every $psi$ gives $f^(**)eta_V=eta_W f$.]
criteria: [State the types of $v,psi$, and the dual maps.]

question: [Classify all natural transformations from the identity functor on sets to itself without using Yoneda.]
hint1: [Use maps from a singleton selecting elements.]
hint2: [The component on a singleton is forced to be its identity.]
solution: [Let $eta$ be natural. For $x in X$, let $i_x:1 -> X$ select $x$. The only function $1 -> 1$ is the identity, so naturality gives $eta_X(x)=eta_X i_x(*)=i_x eta_1(*)=x$. Thus every component is the identity, including the unique map on the empty set. The identity family is natural, so it is the only one.]
criteria: [Handle arbitrary elements via naturality, not a choice of ordering.]

question: [Identify the natural endomorphisms of the identity functor of a group regarded as a one-object category.]
hint1: [A component is a group element.]
hint2: [Naturality says it commutes with every group arrow.]
solution: [A transformation is an element $z in G$ with $g z=z g$ for every $g$. Thus its elements are exactly $Z(G)$. Vertical composition is multiplication of these components, and every component is invertible, so these transformations form the center as a group.]
criteria: [Describe both the set of transformations and its composition.]

question: [Show every natural endomorphism of the identity functor on $K$-vector spaces is multiplication by a single scalar.]
hint1: [Evaluate the component on the one-dimensional space at one.]
hint2: [Use the linear map $K -> V$ taking one to a chosen vector.]
solution:
[*Finding the approach.* Use a one-dimensional test object. Every vector is the image of its distinguished element under a linear map, so naturality propagates one scalar to every space.

*Argument.* Let $c=eta_K(1)$. For $v in V$, the map $i_v:K -> V$, $a |-> a v$, is linear. Naturality gives $eta_V(v)=eta_V i_v(1)=i_v eta_K(1)=c v$. Thus all components use the same scalar. Conversely scalar multiplication commutes with every linear map, so every $c in K$ yields such a transformation.

Naturality of $i_v$ is the equation $eta_V compose i_v=i_v compose eta_K$. Evaluating at one is legitimate because both sides are functions from $K$ to $V$. The scalar $c$ is chosen once from the component at $K$, not separately for each $V$. The zero vector space causes no exception: it has only one endomorphism and scalar multiplication is that map. Conversely, for any linear $f$, $f(c v)=c f(v)$ verifies the full naturality square.

*A tempting dead end.* Checking that each component is some scalar multiple of the identity does not establish that the scalar is the same for all spaces. Naturality is the compatibility that forces uniformity.

*Hypotheses.* Components and test maps are linear, and the category contains $K$ and all maps $i_v$. Restricting the available test maps could allow more transformations.]
criteria: [Prove the scalar is independent of both the vector and the space.]
idea: [The component at the free one-generator object determines every other component through maps carrying its generator to an arbitrary vector.]

question: [Let $P$ send a set to its power set and a function to direct image. Classify all natural transformations $P => P$ on the category of sets.]
hint1: [First determine what happens to the empty subset and to the full subset of a singleton.]
hint2: [For a nonempty set $A$, use permutations of $A$, its map to a singleton, and its inclusion in a larger set.]
solution:
[*Finding the approach.* Naturality under permutations forces any output attached to the whole set to treat all points alike. A map to the singleton synchronizes the choice across different sets.

*Argument.* Let $eta$ be natural. The unique map from the empty set to $X$ implies $eta_X(emptyset)=emptyset$. Write $S_A=eta_A(A)$ for nonempty $A$. Every permutation of $A$ fixes its full subset, so naturality makes $S_A$ invariant under all permutations. If it contains one point, transpositions show it contains every point; otherwise it is empty. Under the map $A -> 1$, naturality says the direct image of $S_A$ equals $eta_1(1)$, so all nonempty $A$ choose the same case. For an arbitrary subset $B subset X$, inclusion $i:B -> X$ gives $eta_X(B)=i(eta_B(B))$. Therefore either every subset is sent to itself, or every subset is sent to the empty set. Both operations commute with direct images, so these two transformations are exactly the answer.

*A tempting dead end.* Testing only bijections permits choices depending on cardinality. Naturality under all functions removes those extra choices.

*Hypotheses.* The power-set functor is covariant by direct image. The proof would be a different problem for inverse image on the opposite category.]
criteria: [Include empty subsets, nonempty sets, arbitrary inclusions, and verification of both resulting transformations.]
idea: [Use symmetry to limit local possibilities, then noninvertible maps to force one global choice.]

question: [Identify initial and terminal objects in sets and in groups.]
hint1: [Ask for unique maps in each direction.]
hint2: [In groups, the trivial group serves both purposes.]
solution: [In sets, the empty set is initial and any singleton is terminal. In groups, the trivial group is initial because its identity must map to the identity, and terminal because there is one homomorphism sending every element to the identity.]
criteria: [Explain uniqueness, not only existence.]

question: [Describe the product of a two-element set and a three-element set with its projections.]
hint1: [Use ordered pairs.]
hint2: [The projections extract the two coordinates.]
solution: [The Cartesian product has six pairs. The maps $(a,b) |-> a$ and $(a,b) |-> b$ are its projections. For maps $f:X -> A,g:X -> B$, the unique mediator is $x |-> (f(x),g(x))$.]
criteria: [Include the universal property.]

question: [Why is ordinary union not always a coproduct of two sets?]
hint1: [Consider two singleton sets with the same element.]
hint2: [The two copies must be allowed to receive different images.]
solution: [If $A=B=\{*\}$, ordinary union is a singleton. Two maps from $A,B$ into a two-element target can send their elements to different values, and no map from the singleton union can extend both. A tagged disjoint union has two elements and does satisfy the coproduct property.]
criteria: [Use incompatible maps to demonstrate failure.]

question: [Find the product and coproduct of twelve and eighteen in positive integers ordered by divisibility.]
hint1: [Products are greatest lower bounds and coproducts least upper bounds.]
hint2: [Use gcd and lcm.]
solution: [The product is six and the coproduct is thirty-six. The universal properties are exactly: common divisors divide the gcd, and the lcm divides every common multiple.]
criteria: [Translate the arrow direction into divisibility.]

question: [Prove two products of fixed objects are uniquely isomorphic compatibly with their projections.]
hint1: [Construct maps in both directions using universality.]
hint2: [Their composites have the same projections as the identities.]
solution: [The projections of each product provide a competing pair of maps for the other, yielding unique comparison maps. Each composite preserves both original projections, as does the identity. The uniqueness clause forces these composites to be identities. The comparison map is unique because its projections were prescribed.]
criteria: [Compatibility with projections is essential to the uniqueness claim.]

question: [Prove $V oplus W$ is both a product and a coproduct in vector spaces.]
hint1: [Use coordinate projections and inclusions.]
hint2: [The mediators are pairing and addition of images.]
solution: [For a product, send $x$ to $(f(x),g(x))$; linearity and uniqueness follow coordinatewise. For a coproduct, send $(v,w)$ to $a(v)+b(w)$; this is linear and extends the given maps on the two summands. Every vector is $(v,0)+(0,w)$, so this extension is unique.]
criteria: [Give both universal properties with their different arrow directions.]

question: [Construct the linear extension of a function from $\{a,b\}$ into a vector space, taking $a$ to $u$ and $b$ to $v$.]
hint1: [Use linearity on the two basis vectors.]
hint2: [A vector has unique coordinates $r[a]+s[b]$.]
solution: [The unique extension sends $r[a]+s[b]$ to $r u+s v$. This formula is linear, has the specified basis values, and is forced by linearity for every input.]
criteria: [Explain uniqueness using the basis expansion.]

question: [Show $A times 1$ is isomorphic to $A$ whenever $1$ is terminal and the product exists.]
hint1: [Pair the identity with the unique map to one.]
hint2: [This pairing is inverse to the first projection.]
solution: [Let $p:A times 1 -> A$ and $s=chevron.l 1_A,!chevron.r:A -> A times 1$. Then $p s=1_A$. Both $s p$ and the identity on the product have first projection $p$ and the unique second projection to one; product uniqueness gives $s p=1$. Thus they are inverse.]
criteria: [Use terminal uniqueness for the second-coordinate comparison.]

question: [Explain why $C_2 times C_2$ with its coordinate inclusions is not a coproduct of two copies of $C_2$ in groups.]
hint1: [Map the two generators to noncommuting involutions in $S_3$.]
solution: [Choose the involutions $(12),(23)$ in $S_3$. Each defines a homomorphism $C_2 -> S_3$. If a map from $C_2 times C_2$ extended both, the two commuting coordinate generators would map to commuting elements. But $(12)(23)!=(23)(12)$. Hence no such extension exists, violating the coproduct property.]
criteria: [Use a target and two valid homomorphisms for which extension fails.]

question: [Construct the canonical isomorphism $(A times B)times C -> A times(B times C)$ solely from universal properties.]
hint1: [Specify its three coordinate composites.]
hint2: [Build nested pairings, then compare the coordinates of the two composites.]
solution: [From the source, take its $A,B,C$ coordinate maps $a,b,c$. Pair $b,c$ to get a map to $B times C$, then pair this with $a$. Construct the reverse map by pairing the first two coordinates. Each composite has the same three coordinate maps as the identity; two successive uses of product uniqueness force equality. Thus the maps are inverse and uniquely compatible with coordinates.]
criteria: [Avoid element notation unless specializing to sets.]

question: [For countably many copies of $K$, show the finite-support direct sum is a coproduct but generally not the product under its coordinate projections.]
hint1: [Maps out of a direct sum use finite sums.]
hint2: [A cone from $K$ with every coordinate the identity would require an all-ones vector.]
solution: [Given linear maps from each copy of $K$ to $V$, send a finite-support tuple to the finite sum of its coordinate images. This defines the unique linear extension, proving the coproduct property. If the same object were a product, the cone from $K$ with every coordinate identity would yield a map sending one to a tuple whose every coordinate is one. This tuple has infinite support and is absent, a contradiction.]
criteria: [Exhibit the cone whose mediator does not exist.]

question: [Prove product projections jointly determine every arrow into the product. Deduce the naturality of the canonical swap $A times B -> B times A$ in both variables.]
hint1: [Use uniqueness for the first claim.]
hint2: [Both naturality-square composites have the same two projections.]
solution:
[*Finding the approach.* Universal properties prove equality without element notation. Test the proposed equality by the projections that characterize the product.

*Argument.* If two arrows into a product have identical projection composites, both mediate the same pair of arrows, so they are equal. The swap is the pairing of the second and first projections. For maps $f:A -> A',g:B -> B'$, the composites $"swap"(f times g)$ and $(g times f)"swap"$ both have projections $g pi_B$ and $f pi_A$. Joint detection makes them equal, proving naturality.

Write $s_(A,B)=⟨ pi_B,pi_A ⟩$. The first projection of either candidate arrow into $B' times A'$ is $g pi_B$, and the second is $f pi_A$. The product property says there is exactly one arrow with those two composites, so the candidates agree. Existence alone is not enough: uniqueness is the part that detects equality. This argument works even in a category whose objects have no underlying elements.

*A tempting dead end.* An equation that resembles swapping coordinates in sets is not a proof in an arbitrary category. Likewise, agreement after just one projection generally leaves the other component undetermined.

*Hypotheses.* Both relevant products must exist and their projections must be fixed. No chosen equality between different constructions of the product is required.]
criteria: [Describe both projected composites with their types.]
idea: [Prove a map equality by showing that both maps solve the same uniquely solvable universal problem.]

question: [In the category of pointed sets and basepoint-preserving functions, construct the coproduct of two finite pointed sets of sizes $m,n$. Prove its universal property, compute its size, and compare it with their product.]
hint1: [Start with a disjoint union, but consider what every basepoint-preserving map must do to its two distinguished points.]
hint2: [Identify exactly the two basepoints, and no other elements.]
solution:
[*Finding the approach.* The disjoint union gives separate choices of values, but a pointed target forces agreement at the two distinguished points. Enforce only that necessary identification.

*Argument.* Take the disjoint union of $A$ and $B$ and identify their basepoints to a single point $*$. The two canonical maps preserve basepoints. Given pointed maps $f:A -> X$ and $g:B -> X$, define the mediator on the first summand by $f$ and on the second by $g$. It is well defined at the identified pair because both values are the basepoint of $X$. Every equivalence class has a representative in one of the summands, so these rules also force uniqueness. The coproduct has $m+n-1$ elements. The product is $A times B$ with basepoint $(a_0,b_0)$ and the usual projections: a pair of pointed maps uniquely gives the pointed pairing. Its size is $m n$. For $m=n=2$, the two sizes are three and four, so these objects cannot be isomorphic.

*A tempting dead end.* A plain disjoint union has two candidate basepoints and cannot make both inclusions pointed without the identification. A Cartesian product solves an incoming-map problem instead.

*Hypotheses.* Pointed sets are nonempty, and all maps preserve the chosen point. Universal properties must use the morphisms of this category.]
criteria: [Give the mediator, prove it is well defined and unique, and compare the two directions of universality.]
idea: [Read the compatibility required by the maps, then impose exactly the relation that makes those maps glue.]

question: [Find the equalizer in sets of $f,g:ZZ -> ZZ$, $f(n)=n^2,g(n)=n$.]
hint1: [Solve the equality of the two values.]
hint2: [The equation is $n(n-1)=0$.]
solution: [The equalizer is the inclusion $\{0,1\} -> ZZ$. Any function whose composites with $f,g$ agree has all values in this subset and factors uniquely through its inclusion.]
criteria: [Give the structural map and universal factorization.]

question: [Find the pullback of $f:ZZ -> ZZ$, $f(a)=2a$, and $g:ZZ -> ZZ$, $g(b)=3b$, in sets.]
hint1: [Solve $2a=3b$.]
hint2: [Coprimality implies $a=3k,b=2k$.]
solution: [The pullback is the set $\{(3k,2k):k in ZZ\}$ with coordinate projections. It can be identified with $ZZ$ by $k |-> (3k,2k)$. Compatibility of any pair of functions forces each value to be such a pair, giving the unique mediator.]
criteria: [Distinguish the abstract apex from its two projection maps.]

question: [In sets, coequalize the two maps from a singleton to $\{a,b,c\}$ selecting $a$ and $b$.]
hint1: [Identify only what the maps force.]
hint2: [The equivalence classes are $\{a,b\}$ and $\{c\}$.]
solution: [The coequalizer is the quotient onto the classes $\{a,b\}$ and $\{c\}$. A map from $\{a,b,c\}$ coequalizes the pair exactly when its values at $a,b$ agree, exactly the condition for a unique map from this quotient.]
criteria: [Describe the factorization condition.]

question: [Explain why a limit of the empty diagram is terminal and a colimit is initial.]
hint1: [There is one empty family of maps for every apex.]
hint2: [The mediator must therefore be unique for every object.]
solution: [A cone over the empty diagram has no structural arrows or compatibility conditions. Its universal property asks for a unique arrow from each object to the chosen apex, which is terminality. Reversing arrows gives initiality for the colimit.]
criteria: [Explain why no extra cone data remain.]

question: [Prove an equalizer arrow is monic using only its universal property.]
hint1: [Consider two maps with the same composite through the equalizer.]
hint2: [They are mediators of the same equalizing arrow.]
solution: [For equalizer $e:E -> A$, if $e u=e v$, this common composite equalizes the original pair. Both $u,v$ factor it through $e$, so uniqueness of the factorization yields $u=v$.]
criteria: [Do not assume the category has elements.]

question: [Prove a pullback of a monomorphism is monic.]
hint1: [Use the two projections to compare arrows into the pullback.]
hint2: [Cancel the original monomorphism to obtain equality of the other projected composites.]
solution: [Let the pullback square have $p:P -> A,q:P -> B$, with $f:A -> C$ monic and $f p=g q$. If $q u=q v$, then $f p u=g q u=g q v=f p v$, so $p u=p v$. Both projected composites now agree, and pullback uniqueness gives $u=v$. Thus $q$ is monic.]
criteria: [Identify which projection is the pullback of the given mono.]

question: [Prove the coequalizer of linear maps $f,g:V -> W$ is $W slash "im"(f-g)$.]
hint1: [A linear map coequalizes exactly when it kills the difference.]
hint2: [Use the universal property of a quotient vector space.]
solution: [For $h:W -> X$, the condition $h f=h g$ is equivalent to $h(f-g)=0$, hence to $"im"(f-g) subset.eq ker h$. This is exactly the condition for a unique linear factor through the quotient map. Thus the quotient has the coequalizer property.]
criteria: [Prove the equivalence of the equations and the kernel condition.]

question: [Compute the pushout of inclusions $\{b\} -> \{a,b\}$ and $\{b\} -> \{b,c\}$ in sets.]
hint1: [Start with a tagged disjoint union.]
hint2: [Identify the two copies of $b$.]
solution: [The resulting set has three elements represented by $a,b,c$. The two inclusion maps agree on the common $b$. Any pair of maps from the original sets agreeing at $b$ determines one function on these three elements and conversely, proving universality.]
criteria: [Begin with distinct tagged copies before imposing the identification.]

question: [Show the equalizer of group homomorphisms $f,g:G -> H$ is a subgroup of $G$. Must it be normal?]
hint1: [Test $a b^(-1)$ for elements with equal images.]
hint2: [For failure of normality compare an inner automorphism with the identity.]
solution: [If $f(a)=g(a)$ and $f(b)=g(b)$, then $f(a b^(-1))=f(a)f(b)^(-1)=g(a)g(b)^(-1)=g(a b^(-1))$, proving subgroup closure. It need not be normal: in $S_3$, the equalizer of conjugation by $(12)$ and the identity is its centralizer $\{e,(12)\}$, which is not normal.]
criteria: [Distinguish a general equalizer from a homomorphism kernel.]

question: [Construct the pullback of $f:A -> C,g:B -> C$ using a product and an equalizer.]
hint1: [Compare two arrows from $A times B$ to $C$.]
hint2: [Equalize $f pi_A$ and $g pi_B$.]
solution: [Let $e:P -> A times B$ equalize $f pi_A,g pi_B:A times B->C$. The composites $pi_A e,pi_B e$ form a compatible square. A compatible pair $u:X -> A,v:X -> B$ gives a unique product map $chevron.l u,v chevron.r$ that equalizes the two maps, hence factors uniquely through $e$. This is precisely the pullback property.]
criteria: [Use both universal properties in sequence and track uniqueness.]

question: [Give a coequalizer in sets where the initially required identification pairs are not themselves transitive, and compute the actual quotient.]
hint1: [Use maps from a two-element set.]
hint2: [Require $a~b$ and $b~c$.]
solution: [Take $A=\{0,1\}$, $B=\{a,b,c\}$, with $f(0)=a,g(0)=b$ and $f(1)=b,g(1)=c$. The listed pairs do not include $a~c$, but any coequalizing function has $h(a)=h(b)=h(c)$. Thus all three elements must be identified, giving a singleton quotient.]
criteria: [Explain why transitive closure is forced by equality in every target.]

question: [Prove that two horizontally composable pullback squares have a pullback as their outer rectangle.]
hint1: [Factor a compatible pair through the right square first.]
hint2: [Then use the left square; reverse this reasoning for uniqueness.]
solution:
[*Finding the approach.* Introduce a general test object and solve its compatibility equations one square at a time. The order matters: the right square supplies the intermediate data needed by the left.

*Argument.* Given maps to the outer lower-left and upper-right corners whose composites to the lower-right agree, compose the first map to the lower-middle corner. The right pullback gives a unique map to the upper-middle corner. Its compatibility with the lower-left map is now exactly the hypothesis for the left pullback, yielding a map to the upper-left corner. Any outer mediator must give the same middle map by right-square uniqueness and then the same left map by left-square uniqueness. Thus the outer square is a pullback.

Name the top row $A -> B -> C$ and the bottom row $D -> E -> F$. Given $x:T -> D$ and $z:T -> C$ with equal composites into $F$, the right square yields $y:T -> B$ with lower composite equal to the image of $x$ in $E$ and right composite $z$. The left square then yields $w:T -> A$ with projections $x,y$. For uniqueness, any competing $w'$ has a $B$-composite solving the same right-square problem, so it equals $y$; left-square uniqueness then gives $w'=w$.

*A tempting dead end.* Proving that the outside rectangle commutes establishes only a cone, not a universal cone. Omitting uniqueness is a common incomplete proof.

*Hypotheses.* Both inner squares are pullbacks and the two rows compose in the indicated direction. The result does not assert that an arbitrary factor of a pullback rectangle is a pullback.]
criteria: [Specify the order of the two factorizations and both uniqueness steps.]
idea: [Factor the universal mapping problem through the shared edge and apply uniqueness in the same order.]

question: [Fix a positive integer $n$. Find an abelian group $P$ and maps $p,q:P -> ZZ$ with $p$ congruent to $2q$ modulo $n$, such that every pair $f,g:A -> ZZ$ with this congruence factors uniquely through $p,q$. Give a basis for $P$.]
hint1: [Describe a pair of compatible integers by their difference $x-2y$.]
hint2: [Write $(x,y)=(n k+2y,y)$.]
solution:
[*Finding the approach.* Translate the congruence into an exact equation with an extra integer. That parameter should both describe the universal object and give its basis.

*Argument.* Let $P=\{(x,y) in ZZ^2:n | (x-2y)\}$, a subgroup under coordinatewise addition, and take coordinate projections. Given $f,g$, the only possible mediator is $h(a)=(f(a),g(a))$. The congruence ensures it lands in $P$; the coordinate formulas show it is a homomorphism. Its two projections prescribe every value, proving uniqueness. Each element of $P$ is uniquely $k(n,0)+y(2,1)$ because $k=(x-2y)/n$ is an integer. Thus the two displayed vectors form a basis and $P iso ZZ^2$. Under these coordinates $p(k,y)=n k+2y$ and $q(k,y)=y$.

*A tempting dead end.* Choosing $P=ZZ^2$ with its standard projections ignores the congruence. Choosing only the pairs $(2y,y)$ imposes equality and excludes legitimate multiples of $n$.

*Hypotheses.* The positive integer $n$ ensures the integer parameter is unique. The universal property quantifies over all abelian groups $A$, not only over individual integer pairs.]
criteria: [Prove closure, both existence and uniqueness of mediation, and independence of the two basis vectors.]
idea: [Parametrize the compatibility equation and verify that the resulting parameterization respects all test maps.]

question: [For $eta:cal(C)(A,-) => F$, which element determines $eta$ under Yoneda?]
hint1: [Evaluate at the representing object.]
hint2: [Use its identity arrow.]
solution: [It is $eta_A(1_A) in F A$. Naturality reconstructs each value by $eta_B(f)=F(f)(eta_A(1_A))$.]
criteria: [Include the reconstruction formula.]

question: [Show the identity functor on sets is covariantly represented by a singleton.]
hint1: [A function from a singleton selects an element.]
hint2: [Evaluate at its unique point.]
solution: [The bijection $"Set"(1,X) -> X$ sends $f$ to $f(*)$. Its inverse sends $x$ to the selecting function. Postcomposing with a function $X -> Y$ corresponds to applying it to the selected element, so the bijection is natural.]
criteria: [Verify naturality, not only cardinality.]

question: [Let $x in F A$. Define the corresponding transformation from $cal(C)(A,-)$ to $F$.]
hint1: [Apply $F$ to a map from $A$.]
hint2: [The component at $B$ sends $f$ to $F(f)(x)$.]
solution: [Define $eta_B(f)=F(f)(x)$. For $g:B -> C$, $F(g)eta_B(f)=F(g f)(x)=eta_C(g f)$, so the family is natural.]
criteria: [Give its formula and naturality check.]

question: [For the underlying-set functor on groups represented by $ZZ$, identify a universal element.]
hint1: [A map from $ZZ$ is determined by one generator.]
hint2: [Choose the integer one.]
solution: [The universal element is $1 in ZZ$. Every $g in G$ is the image of one under the unique homomorphism $n |-> g^n$. This is exactly the universal-element property.]
criteria: [State the unique homomorphism explicitly.]

question: [Classify natural transformations $X times X -> X$ in sets.]
hint1: [Represent pairs by maps from a two-element set.]
hint2: [Yoneda gives one transformation for each element of that set.]
solution: [The functor $X times X$ is naturally $"Set"(2,X)$. Yoneda identifies its transformations to the identity with the two elements of $2$. Reconstruction evaluates a map $2 -> X$ at the selected element, giving exactly the two projections.]
criteria: [Explain the representable identification and reconstructed operations.]

question: [Given $f:A -> B$, write the natural transformation $cal(C)(-,A) => cal(C)(-,B)$ and prove naturality.]
hint1: [Postcompose by $f$.]
hint2: [Precomposition with a test arrow commutes by associativity.]
solution: [At $X$, send $u:X -> A$ to $f u:X -> B$. For $k:Y -> X$, $(f u)k=f(u k)$, so the square with the contravariant hom-functor maps commutes.]
criteria: [Keep the test-arrow direction explicit.]

question: [Show a universal element of a covariant functor is an initial object in its category of elements.]
hint1: [Unpack arrows in the category of elements.]
hint2: [Such an arrow is exactly a map satisfying $F(f)(u)=x$.]
solution: [From $(A,u)$ to $(X,x)$, the category of elements permits precisely arrows $f:A -> X$ with $F(f)(u)=x$. Universality gives exactly one such arrow for every target object, which is the definition of initiality. The same unpacking proves the converse.]
criteria: [State both directions.]

question: [Classify natural transformations from the constant singleton functor on sets to the identity functor.]
hint1: [The constant singleton functor is represented by the empty set.]
hint2: [Yoneda asks for an element of the empty set.]
solution: [Since $"Set"(emptyset,X)$ is always a singleton, Yoneda identifies the transformations with elements of $emptyset$, so there are none. Directly, the component at the empty set would have to be a function $1 -> emptyset$, which does not exist.]
criteria: [Give either full argument and recognize the empty-set obstruction.]

question: [Prove that naturally isomorphic contravariant representables have isomorphic representing objects.]
hint1: [Use fullness of the Yoneda embedding on the isomorphism and its inverse.]
hint2: [Faithfulness translates their composite identities back to arrows.]
solution: [If $h_A iso h_B$, the natural isomorphism and its inverse correspond to arrows $f:A -> B,g:B -> A$. Their composites correspond to identity transformations. Faithfulness of the embedding gives $g f=1_A$ and $f g=1_B$, so $A iso B$.]
criteria: [Explain why the arrows are inverse, not merely that both exist.]

question: [Classify all natural transformations from the underlying-set functor on groups to itself.]
hint1: [It is represented by $ZZ$.]
hint2: [An integer $n$ produces the operation $g |-> g^n$.]
solution: [Yoneda identifies these transformations with the underlying set of $ZZ$, so each corresponds to one integer $n$. For $g in G$, use the homomorphism $f_g:ZZ -> G$ sending one to $g$. Reconstruction gives $eta_G(g)=f_g(n)=g^n$. Every such power operation is natural because homomorphisms preserve integer powers. The component functions need not themselves be homomorphisms.]
criteria: [State the last distinction; the target category of the functor is sets.]

question: [Show the constant empty-set functor from sets to sets is not covariantly representable.]
hint1: [Evaluate a supposed representation at its representing object.]
hint2: [Every object has an identity arrow.]
solution: [If it were represented by $A$, then $"Set"(A,A)$ would be in bijection with the empty set. But it contains $1_A$, even when $A$ is empty. This contradiction proves nonrepresentability.]
criteria: [Use the identity argument for every possible representing set.]

question: [For finite sets $m,n$, classify natural transformations $X^n -> X^m$ on sets, including the empty cases.]
hint1: [Use the covariant representables $"Set"(n,-)$ and $"Set"(m,-)$.]
hint2: [Yoneda identifies transformations with functions $m -> n$.]
solution:
[*Finding the approach.* Tuples are functions out of an indexing set. This turns a claim about operations on every set into a claim about one finite test set.

*Argument.* Yoneda gives $"Nat"("Set"(n,-),"Set"(m,-)) iso "Set"(m,n)$. A function $s:m -> n$ sends an $n$-tuple $x$ to the $m$-tuple $j |-> x(s(j))$, so all operations select and repeat coordinates. If $m$ is empty there is one transformation; if $n$ is empty and $m$ is nonempty there are none. If both are empty there is one.

Evaluate a proposed transformation at the identity tuple $id_n:n -> n$. Its value is a function $s:m -> n$. For any tuple $x:n -> X$, naturality with respect to $x$ forces the transformed tuple to be $x compose s$. Conversely this formula commutes with every map $X -> Y$, proving existence. When $n$ is empty and $m$ is nonempty, evaluating at $X=emptyset$ would require a function from a singleton to the empty set, so no transformation can exist.

*A tempting dead end.* Allowing an arbitrary constant coordinate would require choosing an element of every set naturally, including the empty set. The formula must select an existing input coordinate instead.

*Hypotheses.* The operations are natural with respect to every function of sets. Restricting the category or excluding the empty set changes which arguments are available.]
criteria: [Explain the reversed direction and all empty-set cases.]
idea: [Evaluate at the generic tuple to recover the entire operation, including all empty-index boundary cases.]

objective: "U6 Transfer: Families of subsets from pairs"
question: [For a function $f:X -> Y$, define $P(f)(S)=f[S]$ and $P(P(f))(cal(A))=\{f[S]:S in cal(A)\}$. Classify all families $theta_X:X times X -> P(P(X))$ satisfying $P(P(f))(theta_X(x,y))=theta_Y(f(x),f(y))$ for every $f$. How many such families are there?]
hint1: [Study the ordered pair of distinct elements in a two-element set. Keep a family of subsets distinct from a single subset.]
hint2: [The value at the generic pair is any collection of subsets of that two-element set. Transport the whole collection by direct image.]
solution:
[*Finding the approach.* Each pair is the image of one generic pair, but the output now has two levels of set structure. Naturality transports a collection of subsets, including its possible empty member.

*Argument.* Put $D=\{0,1\}$ and $cal(A)=theta_D(0,1) subset.eq P(D)$. For each $x,y in X$, let $u:D -> X$ send zero to $x$ and one to $y$. Naturality forces $theta_X(x,y)=\{u[S]:S in cal(A)\}$. Conversely, for any fixed collection $cal(A)$ this formula is natural: applying $f$ to each subset gives precisely the subsets $(f compose u)[S]$, which is the formula for the pair $(f(x),f(y))$. Distinct collections give distinct values at $(0,1)$ in D. There are four subsets of D and thus $2^4=16$ collections. For example, the empty collection gives $emptyset$, the collection containing only the empty subset gives $\{emptyset\}$, and $\{\{0\},\{1\}\}$ gives $\{\{x\},\{y\}\}$. When $x=y$, that last output has one member, as direct image requires. The component at the empty set has empty domain and is unique.

*A tempting dead end.* Counting only the four subsets of D ignores the extra power set. Treating $emptyset$ and $\{emptyset\}$ as the same value also loses a distinct natural family. Defining a separate rule for equal inputs generally fails under functions identifying two points.

*Hypotheses.* Both power-set operations use direct image, and naturality ranges over every function, including identifications. The inputs are ordered, so the two singleton-subset collections remain distinguishable.]
criteria: [Prove determination and naturality, obtain all sixteen collections, and distinguish empty and repeated-input cases.]
idea: [Transport a collection attached to a generic pair through two successive direct-image operations; the extra set layer changes the classification.]

question: [For $F:cal(C) -> cal(D)$ left adjoint to $G$, write the hom-set bijection and the types of the unit and counit components.]
hint1: [Place $F$ on the source side of the target-category hom set.]
hint2: [The unit starts at $C$, the counit ends at $D$.]
solution: [The bijection is $cal(D)(F C,D) iso cal(C)(C,G D)$. The unit has type $eta_C:C -> G F C$ and the counit $epsilon_D:F G D -> D$.]
criteria: [Check every object belongs to the category of the displayed hom set.]

question: [Curry the function $f:ZZ times ZZ -> ZZ$, $f(b,a)=2b-a$.]
hint1: [Fix the first argument.]
hint2: [The result is a function assigning a function.]
solution: [The transpose sends $b$ to the function $a |-> 2b-a$. Uncurrying evaluates that function at $a$, recovering the original formula.]
criteria: [State both the curried type and formula.]

question: [Describe the counit of the product–exponential adjunction in sets.]
hint1: [It evaluates a function at an argument.]
hint2: [The domain is $X^A times A$.]
solution: [The counit is $epsilon_X(f,a)=f(a)$ from $X^A times A$ to $X$. It is the uncurried identity on $X^A$.]
criteria: [Identify the adjunct correspondence producing it.]

question: [Describe the unit of the free-vector-space/forgetful adjunction.]
hint1: [Send a generator to its formal basis vector.]
hint2: [The source is a set, not a vector space.]
solution: [At a set $X$, the unit is $x |-> [x]$ from $X$ to the underlying set of the free vector space $K^(X)$. It is a set function, not a purported linear map on $X$.]
criteria: [Keep the source category clear.]

question: [Prove direct image along $f:X -> Y$ is left adjoint to inverse image on power-set posets.]
hint1: [Translate both inequalities into element membership.]
hint2: [The condition is $f[S] subset.eq T$ iff $S subset.eq f^(-1)[T]$.]
solution: [We need $f[S] subset.eq T$ exactly when $S subset.eq f^(-1)[T]$. The left inclusion says every $s in S$ has $f(s) in T$. This is exactly that every $s in S$ belongs to $f^(-1)[T]$, the right inclusion. Both operations are monotone, and the equivalence gives the poset adjunction.]
criteria: [Check monotonicity and the two-way inclusion equivalence.]

question: [Let $i:ZZ -> RR$ be inclusion as ordered sets. Show $i$ is left adjoint to floor.]
hint1: [Compare an integer with a real number.]
hint2: [For integer $n$, $n<=x$ iff $n<=floor(x)$.]
solution: [Floor is monotone. Since $floor(x)$ is the greatest integer at most $x$, an integer $n$ satisfies $i(n)<=x$ exactly when $n<=floor(x)$. This is the adjunction criterion for posets.]
criteria: [Identify which map is left adjoint; ceiling gives the other adjunction.]

question: [For a vector space $V$, describe the counit $F U V -> V$ and verify the triangle involving the unit on $U V$.]
hint1: [A formal linear combination is evaluated as an actual sum.]
hint2: [A single formal basis vector $[v]$ evaluates to $v$.]
solution: [The counit sends $sum_i a_i[v_i]$ to $sum_i a_i v_i$. The unit on the underlying set sends $v$ to $[v]$. Their composite, after applying the forgetful functor as necessary, sends $v$ to $v$, so $U(epsilon_V)eta_(U V)=1_(U V)$.]
criteria: [Distinguish formal sums from actual vector-space sums.]

question: [Given unit and counit, write the transpose of $h:F C -> D$ and the inverse transpose of $k:C -> G D$.]
hint1: [Use one unit or one counit.]
hint2: [The formulas are $G h eta_C$ and $epsilon_D F k$.]
solution: [The transpose is $G(h)eta_C:C -> G D$. The inverse transpose is $epsilon_D F(k):F C -> D$. Their domains match because the unit lands in $G F C$ and $F(k)$ lands in $F G D$. The triangle identities make the two procedures inverse.]
criteria: [Check the intermediate objects.]

question: [Show the diagonal functor $Delta:cal(C) -> cal(C) times cal(C)$ is left adjoint to the binary-product functor when products exist.]
hint1: [Maps from $(X,X)$ to $(A,B)$ are pairs of maps.]
hint2: [The product universal property supplies the corresponding map into $A times B$.]
solution: [The hom set in the product category is $cal(C)(X,A) times cal(C)(X,B)$. The product property identifies this naturally with $cal(C)(X,A times B)$. This is exactly $Delta tack.l times$, with the product operation regarded as a functor defined by pairing.]
criteria: [Mention naturality of the pairing correspondence.]

question: [Prove the two unit–counit transpose formulas are inverse assuming naturality and the triangle identities.]
hint1: [Expand each round trip.]
hint2: [Move the map past the counit or unit using naturality.]
solution: [For $h$, the round trip is $epsilon_D F G(h)F eta_C=h epsilon_(F C)F eta_C=h$. For $k$, it is $G epsilon_D G F(k)eta_C=G epsilon_D eta_(G D)k=k$. The middle equalities use counit and unit naturality; the final equalities use the corresponding triangle.]
criteria: [Name the naturality instance and triangle used in each direction.]

question: [If $F tack.l G$ and $F' tack.l G'$ are composable adjunctions, prove $F'F tack.l GG'$.]
hint1: [Compose the two hom-set bijections.]
hint2: [Track the order of the right adjoints.]
solution: [For appropriate objects $C,E$, the natural bijections are $cal(E)(F'F C,E) iso cal(D)(F C,G'E) iso cal(C)(C,G G'E)$. Their composite is a bijection natural in both variables, so it is an adjunction. The right adjoints appear in reversed composition order.]
criteria: [Specify the three categories and ensure the functors compose.]

question: [For an adjunction $F:P -> Q$, $G:Q -> P$ of posets, prove $G F$ is monotone, extensive, and idempotent.]
hint1: [The unit says $p<=G F p$.]
hint2: [Use the counit inequality on $F p$ for the reverse idempotence inequality.]
solution:
[*Finding the approach.* The two adjunction inequalities give opposite bounds on the second application of $G F$. Idempotence follows by trapping it between equal endpoints.

*Argument.* Monotonicity follows by composition. The adjunction applied to $F p<=F p$ gives $p<=G F p$. Applying this to $G F p$ gives $G F p<=G F G F p$. The counit gives $F G(F p)<=F p$; applying monotone $G$ gives $G F G F p<=G F p$. Antisymmetry yields equality, proving idempotence.

Extensivity applies to every object, so it can be applied to $G F p$ as well as to $p$. The counit at $F p$ gives the opposite inequality after applying monotone $G$. Finally antisymmetry, not merely transitivity, turns the two inequalities into equality. In a preorder this argument gives equivalence in both directions, rather than literal equality of objects.

*A tempting dead end.* Monotonicity and extensivity alone do not imply idempotence: $n |-> n+1$ on the integers has both properties but is not idempotent.

*Hypotheses.* The functors are monotone maps between posets, and the hom-set adjunction is the stated order equivalence. Antisymmetry is needed for equality.]
criteria: [Use both inequalities and antisymmetry.]
idea: [The unit pushes upward and the counit bounds the second pass downward; together they make a closure operator.]

objective: "U7 Transfer: A relation produces a closure"
question: [Given a relation $R subset X times Y$, let $E(A)$ be the set of points of $Y$ related to some member of $A subset X$. For $B subset Y$, find the greatest subset $U(B) subset X$ with $E(U(B)) subset B$. Prove $A subset U(E(A))$ and $U(E(U(E(A))))=U(E(A))$.]
hint1: [Translate 'greatest' into a condition on each possible point $x$.]
hint2: [Every point related to $x$ must lie in $B$, including the case where $x$ has no related points.]
solution:
[*Finding the approach.* The universal condition on an individual point constructs the greatest permitted subset. An order equivalence then turns the repeated expression into two simple inequalities.

*Argument.* Set $U(B)=\{x in X: "for all" y, x R y => y in B\}$. Then $E(A) subset B$ exactly when $A subset U(B)$: both say every neighbor of each point of $A$ belongs to $B$. Thus $U(B)$ is the greatest allowed subset. Both maps are monotone. Applying the equivalence to $E(A) subset E(A)$ gives $A subset U E(A)$. Applying it to $U(B) subset U(B)$ gives $E U(B) subset B$. With $B=E(A)$, monotonicity of $U$ gives $U E U E(A) subset U E(A)$. Extensivity applied to $U E(A)$ gives the reverse inclusion, proving equality. A point with no neighbors is in every $U(B)$, including $U(emptyset)$.

*A tempting dead end.* Using 'there exists a neighbor in B' for $U$ is too weak: another neighbor could lie outside $B$, violating the required inclusion.

*Hypotheses.* No symmetry or functionality is assumed for the relation. Empty neighbor sets must be treated by the universal quantifier's vacuous truth.]
criteria: [Prove the order equivalence, both inequalities for idempotence, and the empty-neighbor case.]
idea: [The existential image and universal precondition form an order adjunction, whose unit and counit control the second closure step.]

question: [Which of products and coproducts must a right adjoint preserve, when they exist?]
hint1: [Use the limit/colimit distinction.]
hint2: [Products are limits.]
solution: [A right adjoint preserves products because they are limits. No general coproduct-preservation statement follows from being a right adjoint alone.]
criteria: [State the existence qualification and avoid claiming a converse.]

question: [Explain why a right adjoint preserves terminal objects.]
hint1: [Terminal objects are empty limits.]
hint2: [Apply limit preservation.]
solution: [A terminal object is the limit of the empty diagram, so its image under a right adjoint is terminal by the limit-preservation theorem. Equivalently its maps from $X$ correspond by adjunction to the unique map from $F X$ into the original terminal object.]
criteria: [Give one complete justification.]

question: [What is the abelianization of an abelian group?]
hint1: [All commutators are already the identity.]
hint2: [The quotient is by the trivial subgroup.]
solution: [For abelian $A$, every $a b a^(-1)b^(-1)=e$, so the commutator subgroup is trivial and $A^"ab"=A slash\{e\}$ is canonically isomorphic to $A$.]
criteria: [Identify the quotient map under the isomorphism.]

question: [In sets, how many functions are in $B^A$ if $|A|=3$ and $|B|=2$? Explain its role in currying.]
hint1: [Choose the image of each of three inputs.]
hint2: [It is the object representing maps out of a product with $A$.]
solution: [There are $2^3=8$ functions. The natural bijection $"Set"(X times A,B) iso "Set"(X,B^A)$ sends a function of two arguments to its family of functions on $A$.]
criteria: [Include the representing property, not only the count.]

question: [Show $cal(C)(A,-)$ preserves a binary product.]
hint1: [Use the product property with source $A$.]
hint2: [A map into the product is equivalent to a pair of component maps.]
solution: [The comparison map sends $h:A -> B times C$ to $(pi_B h,pi_C h)$. Product universality supplies its inverse, pairing the two arrows. Thus it is a bijection respecting projections, which proves preservation of the product in sets.]
criteria: [Identify the actual comparison map.]

question: [Show the free-vector-space functor does not preserve the terminal set.]
hint1: [Compute the free vector space on one generator.]
hint2: [The terminal vector space has dimension zero.]
solution: [The terminal set is a singleton; its free vector space is one-dimensional. The terminal vector space is zero-dimensional, so the image is not terminal. This does not contradict left-adjoint preservation, which concerns colimits rather than limits.]
criteria: [Explain the direction of the theorem.]

question: [Compute the abelianization of $S_3$.]
hint1: [The commutator subgroup lies in the sign kernel.]
hint2: [A commutator of two transpositions is a nontrivial three-cycle.]
solution: [Sign kills commutators, so $[S_3,S_3] subset.eq A_3$. The commutator of $(12)$ and $(23)$ is a nontrivial three-cycle, which generates $A_3$. Thus equality holds and $S_3^"ab" iso S_3 slash A_3 iso C_2$.]
criteria: [Prove both containments for the commutator subgroup.]

question: [Construct the canonical isomorphism $F(A coproduct B) iso F(A) oplus F(B)$ for free vector spaces.]
hint1: [Send tagged basis vectors to the matching summand.]
hint2: [Use linear extension in both directions.]
solution: [Map a basis vector from the $A$ tag to $([a],0)$ and from the $B$ tag to $(0,[b])$, then extend linearly. The inverse sends each summand basis vector to its tagged basis vector. Both composites are identity on every basis vector, hence on the whole space.]
criteria: [Explain why equality on generators suffices.]

question: [For subsets of $S$, prove $X inter A subset.eq B$ iff $X subset.eq (S without A) union B$.]
hint1: [Consider whether an element of $X$ belongs to $A$.]
hint2: [If it does, the first inclusion forces membership in $B$.]
solution: [If the first inclusion holds and $x in X$, then either $x notin A$ or $x in X inter A subset.eq B$, proving the right inclusion. Conversely if $x in X inter A$, the right inclusion places it in the displayed union, and membership in $A$ excludes its complement, so $x in B$.]
criteria: [Prove both directions by element membership.]

question: [Prove directly through adjunct transposes that a right adjoint preserves an equalizer.]
hint1: [Transpose an arrow equalizing the image pair.]
hint2: [Naturality transfers the equality to the original pair.]
solution: [Let $e:E -> A$ equalize $f,g:A -> B$, and let $u:X -> G A$ satisfy $G f u=G g u$. Its transpose $v:F X -> A$ satisfies $f v=g v$ by naturality. There is a unique $w:F X -> E$ with $e w=v$. Transpose $w$ to $z:X -> G E$; naturality gives $G e z=u$. Any second factor would transpose to a second factor through $e$, impossible. Thus $G e$ is the equalizer.]
criteria: [Include the uniqueness argument after transposing back.]

question: [Prove abelianization is left adjoint to inclusion of abelian groups, including naturality.]
hint1: [Every map to an abelian group kills commutators.]
hint2: [Use uniqueness of quotient factorization under pre- and postcomposition.]
solution: [A homomorphism $f:G -> A$ with $A$ abelian kills each commutator and hence factors uniquely through $G^"ab"$. Conversely composing a map from the quotient with its projection gives such an $f$, and the constructions are inverse. Precomposition by a group homomorphism respects commutators, while postcomposition by an abelian-group homomorphism respects factorization. In each case both routes give the unique factor of the same composite, proving naturality.]
criteria: [Establish the bijection and both variables' compatibility.]

question: [Prove an equivalence of categories preserves all existing small limits.]
hint1: [Move a competing cone to an isomorphic object in the image.]
hint2: [Use fullness to lift its arrows and faithfulness to lift the cone equations.]
solution:
[*Finding the approach.* The target limit must accept cones from objects that are not literally images. Essential surjectivity first replaces such an apex by an isomorphic image object.

*Argument.* Let $F$ be full, faithful, and essentially surjective, and let $L$ be a limit. A cone in the target with apex $X$ can be transferred along an isomorphism $F A iso X$. Fullness lifts its legs to arrows from $A$; faithfulness shows they satisfy the cone equations. Limit universality gives a unique arrow $A -> L$. Applying $F$ and composing with the inverse chosen isomorphism gives a mediator from $X$. Fullness and faithfulness translate any rival mediator back to one in the source, proving uniqueness.

Choose $i:F A -> X$. Compose target cone legs with $i$, lift them using fullness, and use faithfulness to reflect every diagram equation. If $u:A -> L$ is the source mediator, the target mediator is $F(u) compose i^(-1)$. Given a rival $v:X -> F L$, fullness lifts $v compose i$; faithfulness shows its source composites equal the cone legs, so source uniqueness forces it to equal $u$. This also shows the resulting mediator is independent of the auxiliary choice of $i$.

*A tempting dead end.* A fully faithful functor need not preserve limits tested against objects outside its essential image. Essential surjectivity is what allows every target apex to enter the proof.

*Hypotheses.* The source diagram has a small indexing category and its limit exists. The argument proves preservation of existing limits, not creation of limits that were absent.]
criteria: [Explain the roles of all three equivalence properties.]
idea: [Transfer every target cone into the source, solve it there, and transfer uniqueness back along the same isomorphism.]

objective: "U8 Transfer: A quotient that loses a kernel"
question: [On abelian groups define $Q(A)=A slash 2A$, with induced maps. Prove that $Q$ preserves coproducts and coequalizers, but does not preserve all kernels.]
hint1: [Any map from $A$ to a group in which twice every element is zero kills $2A$.]
hint2: [For the failure, examine multiplication by two on $ZZ$.]
solution:
[*Finding the approach.* The quotient has a universal property relative to exponent-two groups. This gives the colimit claims efficiently; an injective map that becomes zero supplies a contrasting kernel example.

*Argument.* Let $B$ satisfy $2B=0$. Every homomorphism $A -> B$ kills $2A$ and factors uniquely through $A slash 2A$. Thus the quotient functor to the full subcategory of exponent-two groups is left adjoint to inclusion. To see preservation in all abelian groups explicitly, $Q(bigoplus_i A_i) iso bigoplus_i Q(A_i)$ by coordinate classes, since elements have finite support. The coequalizer of $f,g:A -> B$ is $B slash "im"(f-g)$. Applying $Q$ gives $B slash ("im"(f-g)+2B)$, also the coequalizer of the induced maps $Q(f),Q(g)$.
