question: [Compute $FV((lambda x.lambda y.x y)z)$ and reduce the term to normal form.]
hint1: [Compute free variables before contraction.]
hint2: [The free $z$ does not conflict with $y$.]
solution: [The free-variable set is $\{z\}$. One beta step gives $lambda y.z y$, which is beta normal because the application head is the variable $z$.]
criteria: [Track scope and establish normality.]

question: [Derive the type $(A->B)->A->B$ and interpret the term as a logical proof.]
hint1: [Introduce a function and its input.]
hint2: [Apply the function to the input.]
solution: [The term $lambda f.lambda a.f a$ has the type: under $f:A->B,a:A$, application gives $B$, and two abstractions discharge the assumptions. It is implication elimination followed by introduction.]
criteria: [Provide the intermediate judgment.]

question: [Give a weakly but not strongly normalizing term, then explain why it cannot be typable in the arrow-only core.]
hint1: [Use an ignored divergent argument.]
hint2: [Combine the explicit infinite path with strong normalization.]
solution: [$(lambda x.lambda y.y)Omega$ reduces at the outside to a normal identity abstraction, but can reduce forever inside $Omega$. The strong-normalization theorem excludes an infinite full beta path from every term typable in the specified arrow-only core. Thus this source term is untypable, though its normal form is typable.]
criteria: [Use the theorem only for the fragment in which it was proved.]

question: [Define vector append on paper and justify its result index in both cases.]
hint1: [Match on the first vector.]
hint2: [Its length recursion follows addition on the first argument.]
solution: [For lengths $m,n$, the output length is $"add"(m,n)$. On nil return the second vector, whose length $n$ is definitionally $"add"(0,n)$. On cons, retain the head and append the tail recursively; the result length is $"suc"("add"(m,n))= "add"("suc"(m),n)$ by definition. Each recursive call decreases the first vector.]
criteria: [State the signature, both clauses, and both conversions.]

question: [In the arrow-only language with sole constant $c:o$, show every closed term of type $o->o$, applied to $c$, reduces to $c$. Explain what this does and does not say about equality of functions.]
hint1: [Type the application and use base-type canonicity.]
hint2: [Testing one closed argument is not a general extensionality rule.]
solution: [Application gives $t c:o$ in the empty context. Normalization, preservation, and classification of closed base normal forms imply $t c ->^* c$. This establishes the stated observation at the only closed base normal datum. It does not assert judgmental equality of all functions: for example $lambda x.x$ and $lambda x.c$ are distinct beta-normal terms and hence not beta convertible, although both send $c$ to $c$.]
criteria: [Give the canonicity argument and the explicit function counterexample.]

question: [Construct the dependent-pair map of #link(label("MM8036-U5.06"))[U5.06] and explain how the same formula acts on total spaces in the set model. Prove it respects the projection to the new base.]
hint1: [The first coordinate determines the target fiber.]
hint2: [Project after mapping and compare with applying $f$ after projection.]
solution: [The term sends $(a,b)$ to $(f(a),g(a)(b))$, whose second coordinate belongs to $B'(f(a))$. In sets this is a function between the two total spaces for exactly the same reason. Projecting its output gives $f(a)$, which equals $f$ applied to the input's first projection. Thus the square of total-space map and base map $f$ commutes pointwise.]
criteria: [Verify fiber typing and the commuting square, not just the output notation.]

question: [Reduce $(lambda x.lambda z.x z)y$ and give its type under $y:A->B$.]
hint1: [No binder conflicts with the argument.]
hint2: [The resulting abstraction applies $y$.]
solution: [The reduction gives $lambda z.y z$. Under $z:A$, application yields $y z:B$, so abstraction gives $A->B$ in the context $y:A->B$.]
criteria: [Supply the context rather than treating the free $y$ as closed.]

question: [Give the type and defining reflexive case of transport in a family $P:A->U_0$.]
hint1: [Specify both endpoints.]
hint2: [At reflexivity it is the identity function.]
solution: [For $a,b:A$ and $p:"Id"_A(a,b)$, transport has type $P(a)->P(b)$. Its reflexive clause sends $u:P(a)$ to $u$. Path induction extends this clause to arbitrary $p$.]
criteria: [Include the direction and the role of path induction.]

question: [Construct a term taking $Sigma_(x:A)(B(x) times C(x))$ to $(Sigma_(x:A)B(x)) times(Sigma_(x:A)C(x))$. Explain why the reverse direction is generally unavailable.]
hint1: [Use the same witness in both output pairs.]
hint2: [Two independent existential witnesses need not coincide.]
solution: [Send $(a,(b,c))$ to $((a,b),(a,c))$. In the reverse direction the two supplied witnesses may differ. For a set-model counterexample, let $A=\{0,1\}$, let $B$ be inhabited only at zero and $C$ only at one. Both separate dependent sums are inhabited, while no index supports both fibers, so the original Sigma is empty. Soundness rules out a uniform reverse construction for all such families.]
criteria: [Give the term and a concrete model showing the missing common witness.]

question: [Prove that mapping the identity function over a vector returns the original vector, using propositional equality.]
hint1: [Induct on the vector.]
hint2: [Use congruence of the fixed-head cons constructor.]
solution: [At nil, map computes to nil and reflexivity proves the equality. At $"cons"(a,v)$, map computes to $"cons"(a,"map"("id",v))$. The induction hypothesis identifies its tail with $v$; congruence under $w mapsto "cons"(a,w)$ gives equality with $"cons"(a,v)$. The result lives in the same length-indexed vector type on both sides.]
criteria: [Preserve the index and identify the congruence function.]

question: [Suppose a closed simply typed term reduces along two paths to $u,v$. Prove $u,v$ have a common normal form of the original type.]
hint1: [Use preservation, normalization, and confluence in different roles.]
hint2: [Normalize both reducts and then compare them.]
solution: [Preservation gives both reducts the original type; closedness is retained by reduction. Strong normalization gives normal reducts $n_u,n_v$. Both are normal forms of the original source, so confluence forces them to be alpha equivalent. Repeated preservation gives that common normal form the original type. The argument uses confluence for agreement and normalization for existence; neither theorem substitutes for the other.]
criteria: [State the role of all three metatheorems.]

question: [Explain why the following inference is invalid: “The set model identifies all proofs of equality; therefore the paper theory may use K, and the labs may omit `--without-K`.” Give a correct relationship among syntax, semantics, and the lab options.]
hint1: [Soundness is one-way, and checker options define the accepted fragment.]
hint2: [A model can validate additional principles that the syntax does not assume.]
solution: [Semantic identification does not reflect back to a syntactic derivation without a suitable completeness theorem. Our intensional syntax uses J and has not assumed K. The set model validates the chosen rules but may forget distinctions between proofs. The labs deliberately check a corresponding restricted fragment with `--without-K`; omitting that flag would change the allowed pattern-matching discipline and would no longer certify the stated course constraint. Their existing proofs do pass with the restriction.]
criteria: [Identify the failed converse and distinguish changing a checker option from proving a new theorem.]

question: [Fully parenthesize $lambda x.x y z$ and $a b(c d)$.]
hint1: [Application associates left.]
hint2: [The abstraction body extends to the right.]
solution: [The terms are $lambda x.((x y)z)$ and $(a b)(c d)$. In the first, the entire application is the body; in the second, $c d$ is one argument.]
criteria: [Show both application groupings and binder scope.]

question: [Compute $FV(lambda x.(x y)(lambda y.y z))$.]
hint1: [Compute each subtree first.]
hint2: [The inner binder removes only its own $y$.]
solution: [The left application has free variables $\{x,y\}$; the inner abstraction has $\{z\}$. Their union is $\{x,y,z\}$; the outer binder removes $x$, giving $\{y,z\}$.]
criteria: [Do not remove the free $y$ in the left subtree.]

question: [Which of $lambda x.lambda y.x$, $lambda a.lambda b.a$, and $lambda a.lambda b.b$ are alpha equivalent?]
hint1: [Track binder positions rather than names.]
hint2: [Does the body refer to the outer or inner binder?]
solution: [The first two are alpha equivalent by fresh renaming of both binders. The third refers to the inner binder, whereas the first two refer to the outer binder; capture-free renaming preserves that relation, so it is not equivalent.]
criteria: [Give the binding reason for the negative answer.]

question: [Compute $(lambda y.x y)[x:=y z]$.]
hint1: [The binder conflicts with a free variable of the argument.]
hint2: [Rename it to fresh $w$.]
solution: [First use $lambda w.x w$. Substitution gives $lambda w.(y z)w$. Both $y$ and $z$ remain free.]
criteria: [A fresh name and preserved free variables are essential.]

question: [Compute $(lambda x.(lambda y.x y)z)[y:=x]$ and explain why the replacement has no effect.]
hint1: [Find the free occurrences of $y$.]
hint2: [Every $y$ in this term is bound.]
solution: [The free-variable set of the term is $\{z\}$. Substitution replaces only free occurrences, so the result is the original term up to alpha equivalence. A mechanical algorithm may rename binders while checking freshness, but that does not change the alpha class.]
criteria: [Do not confuse renaming during an algorithm with a semantic change.]

question: [Prove: if $x in FV(t)$, then $FV(t[x:=u])=(FV(t)without\{x\})union FV(u)$.]
hint1: [Strengthen the usual inclusion by considering whether the variable occurs.]
hint2: [Induct on syntax; in the application case at least one branch contains a free $x$.]
solution: [Induct on $t$. For $t=x$ the formula is immediate. For an application, substitution and free variables distribute over the two branches; any branch without $x$ is unchanged, while at least one branch contributes all of $FV(u)$. Their union is the claimed set. For $t=lambda y.s$, the hypothesis excludes $y=x$; rename $y$ fresh for $u$ and distinct from $x$. Apply induction to $s$ and remove $y$. Freshness leaves $FV(u)$ intact and gives precisely the stated formula. These exhaust the possible cases.]
criteria: [Explain why a substituted occurrence exists and why binder freshness matters.]

question: [If $t$ has free variables among $x_1,dots,x_n$ and each $u_i$ is closed, prove simultaneous substitution of $u_i$ for $x_i$ closes $t$.]
hint1: [Use the free-variable bound.]
hint2: [Closed replacements cannot introduce new free variables.]
solution: [Apply substitution sequentially in any fixed order. Each replacement removes its variable and adds no free variables. Because every replacement is closed, subsequent substitutions cannot alter an earlier replacement. After all $n$ steps the free-variable set is empty; this also agrees with simultaneous substitution.]
criteria: [State why sequential and simultaneous replacement coincide here.]

question: [Verify the substitution-composition law for $t=x y$, $u=y z$, $v=w$, substituting first $x$ then $y$.]
hint1: [Check $x!=y$ and $x notin FV(w)$.]
hint2: [Evaluate both sides separately.]
solution: [The left side is $((y z)y)[y:=w]=(w z)w$. On the right, $t[y:=w]=x w$ and $u[y:=w]=w z$, so substitution for $x$ again gives $(w z)w$. Freshness is satisfied for distinct $x,y,z,w$.]
criteria: [Record the conditions before using the law.]

question: [Let size count one for each variable, application, and abstraction node. Prove $|t[x:=u]|=|t|+k(|u|-1)$, where $k$ is the number of free occurrences of $x$ in $t$.]
hint1: [Count what happens at each replaced variable leaf.]
hint2: [Renaming changes names but not node counts.]
solution: [Induct on $t$. A variable $x$ contributes $|u|=1+(|u|-1)$; any other variable contributes one with $k=0$. In an application, sizes add plus one and occurrence counts add, giving the formula from the two induction hypotheses. An abstraction binding $x$ has $k=0$ and is unchanged. Any other abstraction may first be renamed fresh; apply induction to its body and add one.]
criteria: [Include the binding-$x$ case and the application node.]

question: [Construct a counterexample to the substitution-composition equation when $x in FV(v)$, even though $x!=y$.]
hint1: [Use $t=y$.]
hint2: [Take $u=z$ and $v=x$ with three distinct names.]
solution: [Choose distinct $x,y,z$ and put $t=y,u=z,v=x$. The left side $(y[x:=z])[y:=x]$ is $x$. The right side $(y[y:=x])[x:=z[y:=x]]$ is $z$. Distinct free variables are not alpha equivalent. Thus the freshness hypothesis on $v$ cannot simply be deleted.]
criteria: [Evaluate both sides and distinguish alpha equivalence from renaming free variables.]

question: [Prove that substitutions for distinct $x,y$ commute if $x notin FV(v)$ and $y notin FV(u)$: $(t[x:=u])[y:=v]=(t[y:=v])[x:=u]$ up to alpha equivalence. Explain why both side conditions are needed.]
hint1: [Apply composition and simplify its replacement term.]
hint2: [Use the unchanged-term lemma on $u[y:=v]$.]
solution: [Composition gives $(t[y:=v])[x:=u[y:=v]]$. Since $y$ is not free in $u$, this is the right side. Without the first condition, take $t=y,u=z,v=x$: the results are $x$ and $z$. Without the second, take $t=x,u=y,v=z$: the results are $z$ and $y$. Choose distinct $x,y,z$ in each example.]
criteria: [Prove the result and test the two conditions independently.]

question: [Use zero-based de Bruijn indices to encode the closed terms $lambda x.lambda y.x(y x)$ and $lambda a.lambda b.a(b a)$. Explain why this representation detects their alpha equivalence, and why a rule for free variables is still needed for open terms.]
hint1: [Index zero denotes the nearest enclosing binder.]
hint2: [The body is $1(0 1)$.]
solution:
[*Finding the approach.* Replace variable names by the distance to the binder that owns each occurrence. Work from the occurrence outward, rather than assigning a permanent number to each spelling.

*Argument.* Both terms encode as two abstractions with body $1(0 1)$. Renaming a bound variable leaves the number of intervening binders unchanged, so alpha-equivalent terms have the same encoding. Conversely, for closed terms the index at each leaf identifies its binder, and choosing fresh names for the binder nodes reconstructs a representative unique up to alpha renaming. An open term has occurrences with no enclosing binder, so indices alone in this convention do not name its free variables; one needs a separate free-name convention or an external context.

In the common body $x(y x)$, the occurrence of y is bound by the nearest abstraction and therefore has index zero. Each x occurrence skips that abstraction to reach the next and has index one. The same binder tree appears in the version using a and b. For a closed encoding, traverse binder nodes and choose mutually fresh names; each numerical leaf then points to an already present binder. For an open term such as $lambda x.y$, the free y points to no binder, so a separate external name or context entry is necessary.

*A tempting dead end.* Assigning an index to a variable name globally ignores shadowing and changing binder depth. The index records a binding relationship at a particular occurrence.

*Hypotheses.* The specified convention is zero-based and the converse statement concerns well-scoped closed terms. Open terms require the stated additional convention.]
criteria: [Explain both directions for closed terms and the limitation for open terms.]
idea: [Forget spellings while preserving the binder tree; alpha equivalence is exactly the structure that remains.]

objective: "U1 Transfer: Two ways to replace names"
question: [For $t=lambda z.x z$, compute first $t[x:=y][y:=z]$ and then the single simultaneous substitution $t[x:=y,y:=z]$. Are the results alpha equivalent? Explain every binder renaming.]
hint1: [Sequential substitution also acts on the result of the preceding substitution.]
hint2: [A simultaneous substitution inserts each specified image once; it does not recursively substitute inside that image.]
solution:
[*Finding the approach.* The two procedures differ in whether the newly inserted y is visited by the second replacement. Capture avoidance must be handled separately from that distinction.

*Argument.* First $t[x:=y]=lambda z.y z$, since the inserted y is not captured by z. Replacing y by the free variable z now requires renaming the bound z to a fresh w; the result is $lambda w.z w$. For the simultaneous substitution, choose w fresh for both images y and z and rename the body to $x w$. Replacing its free x inserts y, and no original free y occurs, so the result is $lambda w.y w$. The results have different free-variable sets, respectively the singleton z and the singleton y; alpha renaming changes bound names only, so they are not alpha equivalent.

*A tempting dead end.* Replacing inside the inserted image y during the simultaneous operation silently turns it into a sequential operation. Keeping the binder z during the second sequential step would instead capture the inserted free z.

*Hypotheses.* The variables x,y,z are distinct and w is fresh. The simultaneous convention substitutes into original free occurrences without recursively processing the replacement terms.]
criteria: [Show the intermediate term, justify freshness, and use free variables to rule out alpha equivalence.]
idea: [Separate capture avoidance from composition of substitutions; correct renaming does not make simultaneous and sequential substitution the same.]

question: [Reduce $(lambda x.x)(lambda y.y)$ to normal form.]
hint1: [Locate the outer redex.]
hint2: [Substitute the argument for $x$.]
solution: [One step gives $lambda y.y$. It has no application with an abstraction as function, so it is beta normal.]
criteria: [Justify normality as well as the reduction.]

question: [Reduce $(lambda x.lambda y.x)y$.]
hint1: [The free argument must remain free.]
hint2: [Rename the inner binder before contraction.]
solution: [Rename the body to $lambda z.x$; contraction then yields $lambda z.y$. The free-variable set is $\{y\}$, whereas the incorrect answer $lambda y.y$ is closed.]
criteria: [Preserve the free occurrence of the argument.]

question: [Let $Delta=lambda x.x x$ and $Omega=Delta Delta$. Show an infinite beta sequence from $Omega$.]
hint1: [Contract its outer redex.]
hint2: [The contractum is identical to the source.]
solution: [$Omega -> Omega -> Omega -> dots$, because substituting $Delta$ into $x x$ gives $Delta Delta$. Repeating this valid step gives an infinite sequence.]
criteria: [A self-loop is a reduction step even though the printed term repeats.]

question: [Compare outermost reduction and call-by-value on $(lambda x.lambda z.z)Omega$.]
hint1: [The function ignores its argument.]
hint2: [Call-by-value evaluates the argument first.]
solution: [Outermost reduction gives $lambda z.z$ in one step. Call-by-value repeatedly reduces $Omega$ and never applies the outer function. Thus existence of a normal form does not ensure termination of every strategy.]
criteria: [Name the strategy restriction causing divergence.]

question: [For $(lambda x.x x)((lambda y.y)z)$, contract either the outer redex or the argument redex first and exhibit a common reduct.]
hint1: [The outer step duplicates the argument.]
hint2: [Reduce both duplicated argument redexes.]
solution: [The outer-first path gives $((lambda y.y)z)((lambda y.y)z)$, then $z((lambda y.y)z)$, then $z z$. The argument-first path gives $(lambda x.x x)z$, then $z z$. Both branches join even though their lengths differ.]
criteria: [List valid one-step moves on both paths.]

question: [Derive uniqueness of beta normal forms up to alpha equivalence from confluence.]
hint1: [Apply confluence to two normal reducts of one term.]
hint2: [A normal term cannot take a positive number of beta steps.]
solution: [If $t ->^* n$ and $t ->^* m$ with both normal, confluence yields $r$ with $n ->^* r$ and $m ->^* r$. Both sequences must have length zero, so $n,r,m$ are equal in the syntax modulo alpha equivalence.]
criteria: [Use normality at the final step, not termination of all terms.]

question: [Show that beta-convertible normal terms are alpha equivalent. You may use Church–Rosser for conversion.]
hint1: [Conversion can contain reversed steps.]
hint2: [Church–Rosser replaces the zigzag by a common reduct.]
solution: [If $n$ and $m$ are convertible, Church–Rosser gives $r$ with $n ->^* r <-^* m$. Their normality forces both paths to be empty, hence their alpha classes agree. A direct appeal only to a common source would be insufficient until the conversion form of the theorem is established.]
criteria: [Distinguish a conversion zigzag from a reduction sequence.]

question: [Prove that $(lambda x.lambda z.z)Omega$ is weakly normalizing but not strongly normalizing under full beta reduction.]
hint1: [Use two different permitted sequences.]
hint2: [Full reduction may reduce inside the ignored argument.]
solution: [A single outer contraction reaches normal form $lambda z.z$, proving weak normalization. Repeatedly contract the occurrence of $Omega$ in the argument without contracting the outside redex; this is an infinite full beta sequence. Hence the term is not strongly normalizing.]
criteria: [Provide witnesses for both assertions.]

question: [Compute the complete development of $(lambda x.x x)((lambda y.y)z)$. Explain why it differs from contracting just one redex.]
hint1: [Develop the body and argument before substituting.]
hint2: [The argument develops to $z$.]
solution: [Using the complete-development clause for a redex, the developed body is $x x$ and the developed argument is $z$, so the result is $z z$. A single outer beta step instead leaves two copies of the argument redex. Parallel development contracts the residual copies represented by the recursively developed argument.]
criteria: [Use the definition recursively rather than treating development as a strategy name.]

question: [Give a finite abstract reduction system that is confluent but has an infinite reduction sequence, and prove both claims.]
hint1: [A self-loop is enough, but add a visible normal form.]
hint2: [Use $a->a$ and $a->b$ with $b$ normal.]
solution: [Take objects $\{a,b\}$ and exactly the rules $a->a$ and $a->b$, with no step from $b$. Every reduct of $b$ is $b$, while a reduct of $a$ is either $a$ or $b$. Any pair of reducts of $a$ joins at $b$; this proves confluence. The sequence repeating $a->a$ is infinite. Thus confluence alone does not imply strong normalization, even when every object has a normal form.]
criteria: [Check all possible source objects and reduct pairs.]

question: [Prove that if $u -> u'$, then $t[x:=u] ->^* t[x:=u']$. Explain why one step is generally insufficient.]
hint1: [Induct on $t$, renaming binders fresh.]
hint2: [There is one copy of the step for each free occurrence of $x$.]
solution: [For $t=x$ use the given step; for another variable use zero steps. In an application, apply the induction sequences in its left and then right subterm. Under a binder other than $x$, rename fresh for $u,u'$ and lift the induction sequence under the abstraction. A binder $x$ blocks substitution and needs zero steps. For $t=x x$, the substitution produces two copies of $u$, so reducing both may require two steps; if $x$ is absent it requires none.]
criteria: [Include zero steps and duplicated occurrences.]

question: [Prove the closed terms $lambda x.lambda y.x$ and $lambda x.lambda y.y$ are not beta convertible. Why is their different behavior on some arguments not needed for this proof?]
hint1: [Inspect normal forms and binding structure.]
hint2: [Combine normal-form uniqueness for conversion with the de Bruijn invariant.]
solution:
[*Finding the approach.* Normal forms provide a syntactic invariant. Check normality and binding structure first, then use confluence to rule out a hypothetical conversion.

*Argument.* Both terms are beta normal. Their encodings have respective bodies $1$ and $0$, so they are not alpha equivalent. If they were beta convertible, Church–Rosser and normality would force alpha equivalence, a contradiction. Operational tests could provide intuition, but this syntactic invariant already proves nonconvertibility without choosing or interpreting arguments.

Neither term contains an application with an abstraction in function position, so neither can take a beta step. Church–Rosser says beta-convertible terms have a common reduct, with terms considered up to alpha renaming. A normal term's only multistep reduct is itself up to that convention. The first body's occurrence points to the outer binder and the second to the inner binder, so they cannot share a reduct.

*A tempting dead end.* Merely observing that two normal terms have different variable names is insufficient, since bound names can be renamed. The different binder positions are the decisive distinction.

*Hypotheses.* The conversion is beta conversion with capture-avoiding substitution. Adding arbitrary new equations could identify terms that beta conversion distinguishes.]
criteria: [Establish normality and failure of alpha equivalence separately.]
idea: [Use confluence to reduce convertibility of normal terms to equality of their binding structures.]

objective: "U2 Transfer: Termination after duplicating an input"
question: [Let $I=lambda z.z$ and $D=lambda x.x x$. Suppose a closed term t reduces in finitely many beta steps to I. Prove that D t has a normal form. Must D t be strongly normalizing for every such t?]
hint1: [First follow the given finite reduction inside the argument of D.]
hint2: [For the second part, an argument can reach I while containing a subterm whose reduction never stops.]
solution:
[*Finding the approach.* The supplied reduction gives one successful strategy, so it proves weak normalization. To test the stronger claim, retain a divergent component that this successful strategy erases.

*Argument.* By closure of beta reduction under contexts, $D t ->^* D I -> I I -> I$, and I is normal. Thus D t is weakly normalizing. Let $Omega=(lambda u.u u)(lambda u.u u)$ and choose $t=(lambda v.I)Omega$. This closed term reduces to I in one outer step. However inside the argument of D, the Omega subterm can reduce to itself forever, producing an infinite full beta-reduction sequence from D t. Hence D t need not be strongly normalizing. Confluence guarantees that a reached normal form agrees with I up to alpha equivalence; it does not rule out the infinite path.

*A tempting dead end.* Existence of a terminating strategy is not termination of every reduction sequence. Confluence also does not convert weak normalization into strong normalization.

*Hypotheses.* This is the untyped calculus with full beta reduction, including reduction inside arguments. No typing claim is made for D or Omega.]
criteria: [Give the finite path, the closed counterexample, its infinite path, and the precise role of confluence.]
idea: [Use the given successful path for existence, then place divergence in a part that another strategy can keep reducing.]

question: [Give a derivation of $lambda x.x:A->A$ in the empty context.]
hint1: [Start with the variable rule.]
hint2: [Discharge $x:A$ by abstraction.]
solution: [The variable rule gives $x:A tack.r x:A$. The abstraction rule then gives $tack.r lambda x.x:A->A$. The premise explicitly contains the assumption discharged by the conclusion.]
criteria: [Show the premise context and discharged assumption.]

question: [In context $f:A->B,x:A$, derive $f x:B$.]
hint1: [Use the variable rule twice.]
hint2: [Apply the arrow elimination rule.]
solution: [The context contains $f:A->B$ and $x:A$, giving both variable judgments. Arrow elimination yields $f x:B$ in the same context. No assumption is discharged.]
criteria: [The argument type must be exactly the arrow domain.]

question: [Give a type and derivation for $lambda x.lambda y.x$.]
hint1: [Arrows associate right.]
hint2: [First abstract over $y$, then $x$.]
solution: [From $x:A,y:B tack.r x:A$, abstract over $y$ to get $x:A tack.r lambda y.x:B->A$, then over $x$ to obtain $A->(B->A)$.]
criteria: [Do not confuse this with $(A->B)->A$.]

question: [Given $x:A tack.r x:A$ and $tack.r u:A$, calculate the conclusion of substitution.]
hint1: [Replace the free variable.]
hint2: [The result type remains $A$ in simple typing.]
solution: [Substitution gives $tack.r x[x:=u]:A$, namely $tack.r u:A$. This smallest instance makes clear that the substituted assumption is removed from the context.]
criteria: [State both the result term and resulting context.]

question: [Derive the type of $lambda f.lambda g.lambda x.f(g x)$ from chosen types $f:B->C,g:A->B$.]
hint1: [Work from the innermost application outward.]
hint2: [Discharge assumptions in reverse order.]
solution: [In context $f:B->C,g:A->B,x:A$, obtain $g x:B$ and then $f(g x):C$. Three abstractions yield $(B->C)->(A->B)->A->C$, with right association throughout.]
criteria: [Show the two intermediate application judgments.]

question: [Prove admissibility of adding a fresh unused variable $y:B$ to a simply typed context.]
hint1: [Induct on the typing derivation.]
hint2: [Rename abstraction binders to remain fresh for the new context.]
solution: [Induct on the original typing derivation. For a variable, its original declaration is still present. The constant rule is context-independent. For application, weaken both premises and apply the same rule. For abstraction, rename its bound variable away from $y$, weaken the body derivation under the extended context, and reapply abstraction. The resulting term and type are unchanged.]
criteria: [Treat the binder case and freshness explicitly.]

question: [Prove preservation for a root redex $(lambda x.t)u -> t[x:=u]$ using inversion and substitution.]
hint1: [Invert application, then abstraction.]
hint2: [The body premise has the exact assumption required by substitution.]
solution: [If $Gamma tack.r (lambda x.t)u:B$, application inversion supplies some $A$ with $Gamma tack.r lambda x.t:A->B$ and $Gamma tack.r u:A$. Abstraction inversion supplies $Gamma,x:A tack.r t:B$. Substitution therefore gives $Gamma tack.r t[x:=u]:B$.]
criteria: [Identify the same domain type in both premises.]

question: [Give a well-typed open term that is neither a call-by-value value nor able to step, under the lecture convention that values are abstractions and the inert base constant.]
hint1: [A neutral application has no visible function constructor.]
hint2: [Use $f:o->o,x:o$.]
solution: [In context $f:o->o,x:o$, the term $f x:o$ is typable. It is not an abstraction or constant. Neither subterm steps, and $f$ is not an abstraction, so no call-by-value rule applies. The closedness assumption in progress prevents this example.]
criteria: [Use the specified value convention and explain all possible step rules.]

question: [Prove $lambda x.x x$ is untypable in finite simple types.]
hint1: [Invert the two uses of $x$ in one context.]
hint2: [Its type would have to equal an arrow having itself as domain.]
solution: [Suppose the declaration of $x$ is $A$. Typing $x x$ requires a type $B$ with $A=A->B$: the function occurrence has type $A->B$, while the argument occurrence has type $A$. A finite simple type has a finite number of constructor nodes, whereas $A->B$ has strictly more nodes than $A$. Thus this equality is impossible.]
criteria: [Explain why one variable cannot receive unrelated types in the same context.]

question: [Construct a beta step from an untypable term to a typable closed term. Prove both typing assertions.]
hint1: [An ignored argument may itself be untypable.]
hint2: [Use $(lambda x.lambda y.y)Omega$.]
solution: [Take $(lambda x.lambda y.y)Omega$. It reduces to $lambda y.y$, typable at $A->A$. If the source were typable, application inversion would make $Omega=Delta Delta$ typable and hence would make $Delta=lambda z.z z$ typable. The finite-type argument of Exercise #link(label("MM8036-U3.09"))[U3.09] rules that out. Thus typing is preserved forward by reduction but need not be reflected backward.]
criteria: [Use inversion to justify untypability of the whole source.]

question: [Prove the application and abstraction cases of the substitution lemma, including why a binder may need renaming.]
hint1: [State the induction hypothesis for each immediate premise.]
hint2: [For an abstraction, choose its binder fresh for the substituting term and distinct from the variable being removed.]
solution: [Assume $Gamma,x:A tack.r t:B$ and $Gamma tack.r u:A$. For an application $s r$, inversion gives $s:C->B$ and $r:C$ under the extended context; induction substitutes in both, and application yields $s[x:=u]r[x:=u]:B$. For $t=lambda y.s$, rename $y$ fresh. Its body has a derivation under $Gamma,x:A,y:C$. Weaken the typing of $u$ by $y:C$, apply induction to the body (using the harmless exchange of distinct simple declarations), then abstract over $y$. Capture avoidance ensures this abstraction is the intended substituted term.]
criteria: [Track contexts and justify weakening rather than assuming the argument is typable under any context.]

question: [Prove that a closed beta-normal arrow-only term of base type $o$, in the language with exactly one inert constant $c:o$, must be $c$.]
hint1: [Classify normal terms into abstractions and neutral spines.]
hint2: [A closed neutral spine must be headed by a constant.]
solution:
[*Finding the approach.* Inspect the head of a normal application spine. Its type must account for every argument, which is very restrictive at base type in an empty context.

*Argument.* A normal term is an abstraction or a variable/constant followed by zero or more arguments: otherwise an application with an abstraction head would be a redex. A term of base type cannot be an abstraction. Closedness excludes a variable at the head of the outer spine. The only constant is $c:o$, which cannot accept an argument because its type is not an arrow. Hence the spine has no arguments and the term is $c$. Bound variables inside possible arguments do not change the absence of a suitable outer head.

If the head were an abstraction with an argument, there would be a beta redex. If the entire term were an abstraction, its type would be an arrow by the typing rule. Thus a base-type normal term has a variable or constant at the head. A variable there would be free because no outer binder remains, contradicting closedness. The sole constant has type o, so application typing forbids even one argument. This exhausts all syntax forms.

*A tempting dead end.* Induction on subterms without tracking the surrounding context may incorrectly rule out bound variables occurring inside arguments. The proof only excludes a variable at the outermost head.

*Hypotheses.* The language has exactly one inert base constant and no additional eliminators, recursion, or constants of function type. Extra constructors could add further closed normal forms.]
criteria: [Use normality, closedness, and the constant's type separately.]
idea: [Combine the normal-form spine shape with closedness and the head's available arrow arguments.]

objective: "U3 Transfer: All normal outputs in a tiny context"
question: [In the arrow-only core with sole constant $c:o$, classify all beta-normal terms of type o in context $f:o->o,x:o$. Prove your list is exhaustive and that distinct listed terms are not beta convertible.]
hint1: [Inspect the head of a normal application spine.]
hint2: [The head can be x, c, or f; only f accepts an argument, again of type o.]
solution:
[*Finding the approach.* Normal-form syntax and the available head types reduce the problem to a finite recursive grammar. Confluence then separates the resulting normal forms.

*Argument.* A term of type o cannot be an abstraction. Its normal head is a variable or the constant. The only possible heads in this context are x, f, and c. The heads x and c have base type and permit no arguments. The head f has exactly one argument, which must itself be a beta-normal term of type o. Recursing on this proper subterm shows the term is $f^n x$ or $f^n c$ for a nonnegative integer n, where powers mean iterated application. Conversely every such term has type o by repeated application and has no beta redex. Distinct choices of n or terminal symbol have different syntax trees and are not alpha equivalent; Church–Rosser therefore prevents beta convertibility between them.

*A tempting dead end.* Because x and c have the same type, they need not be interchangeable terms. Also no arbitrary lambda term can be inserted as the argument of f, whose domain is the base type.

*Hypotheses.* The context and sole constant are exactly as stated. Extra function variables or constants would enlarge the grammar. No eta rule is needed.]
criteria: [Prove the exhaustive recursive shape, typing of every listed form, and nonconvertibility.]
idea: [Use the typing of the head to derive a grammar of normal forms rather than guessing a few examples.]

question: [Write a proof term for $A->B->A$.]
hint1: [Introduce both assumptions.]
hint2: [Return the first assumption.]
solution: [$lambda a.lambda b.a$ has the required type: under $a:A,b:B$ the variable $a$ has type $A$, and two abstractions discharge $b$ then $a$.]
criteria: [Explain assumption discharge.]

question: [Construct $(A times B)->A$ and $(A times B)->B$.]
hint1: [Use product elimination.]
hint2: [Use the two projections.]
solution: [The functions are $lambda p.pi_1(p)$ and $lambda p.pi_2(p)$. On an input pair $(a,b)$ they compute to $a$ and $b$, respectively.]
criteria: [Give their computation on a constructor.]

question: [Construct $A->A+B$ and explain what data the output contains.]
hint1: [Choose the left constructor.]
hint2: [Keep the supplied evidence for $A$.]
solution: [Send $a$ to the left injection of $a$. The output includes both the tag “left” and the evidence $a:A$; no evidence for $B$ is required.]
criteria: [Do not replace a constructive sum by an untagged assertion.]

question: [State weak and strong normalization and their implication relation.]
hint1: [One asks for a successful path; the other quantifies over all paths.]
hint2: [Every infinite path must be excluded for strong normalization.]
solution: [Weak normalization means existence of a finite reduction to a normal form. Strong normalization means absence of every infinite reduction sequence. In the finitely branching term system, strong normalization implies weak normalization by repeatedly choosing a step until none is possible. The converse fails by the ignored-$Omega$ example.]
criteria: [Give the direction and a counterexample to its converse.]

question: [Construct $(A->B)->((B->0)->(A->0))$.]
hint1: [Assume evidence for $A$ and aim at the empty type.]
hint2: [Compose the two functions.]
solution: [The term $lambda f.lambda n.lambda a.n(f a)$ works. Under $f:A->B,n:B->0,a:A$, application first gives $f a:B$ and then $n(f a):0$. Discharging the three assumptions yields the stated type.]
criteria: [This is constructive contraposition; no converse is asserted.]

question: [Construct $((A->C) times(B->C))->((A+B)->C)$ and state its two computation cases.]
hint1: [Project the two functions and inspect the sum.]
hint2: [Apply the function matching the tag.]
solution: [Given pair $(f,g)$, send a left input $a$ to $f a$ and a right input $b$ to $g b$. These clauses are the sum eliminator with constant result type $C$, and its beta rules give exactly those outputs.]
criteria: [Both branches must produce the same target type.]

question: [Explain why every variable belongs to every reducibility candidate defined in Lecture 7.]
hint1: [Use neutral closure, not a typing assignment.]
hint2: [A variable has no immediate reducts.]
solution: [Variables are neutral. The condition that every immediate reduct be reducible holds vacuously because there are no such reducts. Candidate property (3) therefore puts any variable in $cal(R)_A$ for every simple type $A$. This is a property of raw terms; it does not assign all types to a variable in a fixed typing context.]
criteria: [Distinguish reducibility membership from a typing judgment.]

question: [Show that strong normalization of $s$ and $t$ does not imply strong normalization of $s t$.]
hint1: [Use a normal abstraction that duplicates its argument.]
hint2: [Take both terms to be $Delta=lambda x.x x$.]
solution: [Set $s=t=Delta=lambda x.x x$. The term $Delta$ has no beta redex, so each copy is strongly normalizing. Their application is $Omega$, which reduces to itself forever. Thus an application proof needs the arrow candidate condition controlling all reducible arguments, rather than only the termination of the function and argument separately.]
criteria: [Check normality of $Delta$ and divergence of its application.]

question: [Construct $A->((A->0)->0)$ and explain why reversing the arrow requires a different argument.]
hint1: [An assumption of $A$ can be fed to its negation.]
hint2: [Return $lambda n.n a$.]
solution: [The full term is $lambda a.lambda n.n a$. It constructs double-negation evidence from $a:A$. For the reverse direction, an input of type $(A->0)->0$ expects a refuter of $A$; it does not directly supply a term of $A$. The construction just given cannot be run backwards, and the general reverse principle is not adopted as an axiom of the constructive core.]
criteria: [Give the term without claiming that failure to find a reverse term alone proves uninhabitability.]

question: [Using normalization, preservation, and #link(label("MM8036-U3.12"))[U3.12], prove every closed term of type $o$ reduces to $c$ in the arrow-only calculus with sole constant $c:o$.]
hint1: [Each theorem supplies one step in the argument.]
hint2: [Normalize first, preserve the type, then classify the normal form.]
solution: [Strong normalization gives a finite reduction to some normal $n$. Repeated preservation gives $tack.r n:o$, and reduction preserves closedness by the substitution free-variable bound. #link(label("MM8036-U3.12"))[U3.12] classifies such a closed normal term as $c$. Hence the original term reduces to $c$. Confluence additionally shows that any normal form reached is the same, but is not needed to establish existence of this reduction.]
criteria: [Make the closedness and type of the normal form explicit.]

question: [Construct maps in both directions between $(A+B)->C$ and $(A->C) times(B->C)$. Show the composites agree pointwise on constructor inputs.]
hint1: [Restrict a function along each injection; reverse by cases.]
hint2: [Test the resulting functions at left and right inputs.]
solution: [Map $h$ to the pair sending $a$ to $h("inl"(a))$ and $b$ to $h("inr"(b))$. Reverse a pair $(f,g)$ by sum elimination. Starting with $h$, the composite applied to a left input computes to $h("inl"(a))$, and similarly for a right input. Starting with $(f,g)$, its two resulting functions compute at any $a,b$ to $f(a),g(b)$. This proves the asserted pointwise computation behavior; an identity of functions in intensional identity types would require additional reasoning and is not claimed here.]
criteria: [Separate pointwise computation from an assumed function-extensionality principle.]

question: [Reconstruct the abstraction case of the fundamental reducibility lemma. Identify exactly where the controlled beta-expansion lemma is used.]
hint1: [The arrow clause needs strong normalization of the abstraction and reducibility of every application.]
hint2: [Use two environment extensions: a fresh variable and an arbitrary reducible argument.]
solution:
[*Finding the approach.* The arrow candidate asks for two things: termination of the abstraction and good behavior on every reducible argument. Prove these with different environment extensions.

*Argument.* Given a reducible environment for the free context, rename the binder $x$ fresh and let $s$ be its substituted body. Extend the environment by mapping $x$ to a fresh variable. The body induction hypothesis gives a strongly normalizing renamed copy of $s$, hence $s$ and its abstraction are strongly normalizing. For any $u in cal(R)_A$, extend the environment instead by $x:=u$; induction yields $s[x:=u] in cal(R)_B$. Since $s,u$ are strongly normalizing, controlled beta expansion gives $(lambda x.s)u in cal(R)_B$. Both clauses of $cal(R)_(A->B)$ are now satisfied.

The fresh-variable extension gives a renamed version of the substituted body, whose strong normalization transfers back by alpha invariance. Reduction under a lambda is reduction in that body, so the abstraction is strongly normalizing. For the arbitrary-argument extension, freshness ensures simultaneous substitution agrees with first applying the original environment and then substituting the argument for x. This produces exactly the contractum required by controlled beta expansion. That lemma additionally needs the body's and argument's strong normalization; the first extension and candidate property one supply them.

*A tempting dead end.* Using only the arbitrary-argument extension leaves strong normalization of the unreduced body unproved. Saying the contractum terminates does not imply the redex terminates if an erased argument can diverge.

*Hypotheses.* This is proof reconstruction for the arrow-only simply typed core. The substitution is capture avoiding, the binder is fresh for the environment, and no dependent normalization theorem is being claimed.]
criteria: [Supply both environment extensions and both parts of the arrow definition.]
idea: [Separate the fresh-variable termination check from the arbitrary-argument reducibility check, then join them with controlled expansion.]

question: [Let $t in cal(R)_(A->B)$ and $u in cal(R)_(B->C)$, with x fresh for both. Prove that $lambda x.u(t x)$ belongs to $cal(R)_(A->C)$. Do not assume t or u has a typing derivation.]
hint1: [A fresh variable belongs to every candidate.]
hint2: [First prove the body strongly normalizing; then test the abstraction on an arbitrary reducible argument.]
solution:
[*Finding the approach.* The arrow candidate has two obligations. The fresh-variable test establishes the first without a typing assumption, and a general candidate argument establishes the contractum needed for the second.

*Argument.* Since x is neutral with no reducts, $x in cal(R)_A$. The arrow conditions give $t x in cal(R)_B$ and $u(t x) in cal(R)_C$, hence the body is strongly normalizing. The abstraction is therefore strongly normalizing too. Now choose arbitrary $v in cal(R)_A$. Again the arrow conditions give $u(t v) in cal(R)_C$. Freshness of x ensures that substituting v in the body yields exactly this term. Both the original body and v are strongly normalizing, so controlled beta expansion gives $(lambda x.u(t x))v in cal(R)_C$. These are precisely the two clauses defining membership in $cal(R)_(A->C)$.

*A tempting dead end.* Applying the fundamental typing lemma would assume typing derivations not supplied by the question. Knowing only that t and u terminate would not justify their applications to arbitrary arguments.

*Hypotheses.* The candidates are defined on raw terms, x is fresh to avoid altering t or u during substitution, and the controlled expansion lemma is the arrow-core result already proved.]
criteria: [Verify strong normalization and the arbitrary-argument clause separately, and identify every expansion hypothesis.]
idea: [Compose the candidate application guarantees, using one test for the body and another for all arguments.]

question: [State the data needed to form $Pi_(x:A)B(x)$ in context $Gamma$.]
hint1: [The codomain is checked in an extended context.]
hint2: [It may mention the new variable $x$.]
solution: [One needs $Gamma tack.r A$ type and $Gamma,x:A tack.r B(x)$ type. With levels $A:U_i$ and $B(x):U_j$, the product lies in $U_(max(i,j))$. The body family is not required to be constant.]
criteria: [State the extended context and level rule.]

question: [If $f:Pi_(x:A)B(x)$ and $a:A$, what is the type of $f a$?]
hint1: [Substitute the actual argument into the family.]
hint2: [The result lies over $a$.]
solution: [The type is $B(a)$, formally $B(x)[x:=a]$. Using an unrelated fiber $B(b)$ would require additional equality evidence and transport.]
criteria: [Show the dependency in the result type.]

question: [What must be supplied to construct a term of $Sigma_(x:A)B(x)$?]
hint1: [The second component depends on the first.]
hint2: [Supply $a:A$ and then $b:B(a)$.]
solution: [The pair $(a,b)$ inhabits the dependent sum when $a:A$ and $b:B(a)$. An arbitrary $b:B(c)$ cannot be paired with $a$ unless the needed conversion or transport is provided.]
criteria: [State the exact fiber for the second component.]

question: [State the types and computation rules for the projections of $p:Sigma_(x:A)B(x)$.]
hint1: [The second projection's type mentions the first.]
hint2: [Evaluate both projections on $(a,b)$.]
solution: [The first projection has type $A$, and the second has type $B(pi_1(p))$. On a constructor pair, $pi_1(a,b) equiv a$ and $pi_2(a,b) equiv b$, with the second type converting to $B(a)$.]
criteria: [Include dependent typing, not just projection equations.]

question: [Derive the type of $lambda A.lambda x.x$ with $A:U_0$. Determine the level of its type.]
hint1: [The inner identity is small, but the outer domain is a universe.]
solution: [Under $A:U_0,x:A$, the variable rule gives $x:A$. Abstraction twice gives $Pi_(A:U_0)(A->A)$. The inner arrow is in $U_0$, but the outer Pi has domain $U_0$, which belongs to $U_1$; hence the complete type lies in $U_1$.]
criteria: [Do not infer that a quantification over all small types is itself small.]

question: [Given $f:A->A'$ and $g:Pi_(x:A)(B(x)->B'(f x))$, construct a map $Sigma_(x:A)B(x)->Sigma_(y:A')B'(y)$.]
hint1: [Eliminate the input pair.]
hint2: [Send $(a,b)$ to $(f a,g a b)$.]
solution: [On a pair $(a,b)$, form first component $f a:A'$ and second component $g a b:B'(f a)$. The Sigma introduction rule therefore gives the required output pair. Pair elimination extends this definition to every input.]
criteria: [Check the second component against the transformed first component.]

question: [Given $f:Pi_(x:A)B(x)$ and $g:Pi_(x:A)(B(x)->C(x))$, derive a term of $Pi_(x:A)C(x)$.]
hint1: [Work under an arbitrary $x:A$.]
hint2: [Apply $g$ at the same index as $f$.]
solution: [The term is $lambda x.g x(f x)$. In context $x:A$, dependent application gives $f x:B(x)$ and $g x:B(x)->C(x)$, then ordinary application gives $C(x)$. Abstraction closes the derivation.]
criteria: [Keep both functions at the same index.]

question: [Explain the computational difference between $Sigma_(n:"Nat")P(n)$ and $Pi_(n:"Nat")P(n)$, and give their respective elimination uses.]
hint1: [One stores a witness; one accepts an arbitrary input.]
hint2: [Project a Sigma; apply a Pi.]
solution: [A Sigma term contains a particular number and evidence about that number. Its projections yield $n:"Nat"$ and evidence of $P(n)$. A Pi term supplies evidence of $P(n)$ for each requested $n$ and is eliminated by application to a chosen number. A single witness does not establish all instances.]
criteria: [Use the exact types of the extracted evidence.]

question: [Show that Sigma and Pi over constant families reproduce ordinary products and arrows.]
hint1: [Write their introduction, elimination, and computation rules.]
hint2: [The substitution into a constant family changes nothing.]
solution: [If $B(x)=B$ independently of $x$, a Sigma pair has components $a:A,b:B$, its projections have types $A,B$, and their beta rules are those of $A times B$. A Pi term is an abstraction returning $B$, application returns $B$, and its beta rule is ordinary function substitution. Thus these are the dependent constructions specialized to constant families, subject to the chosen eta rules of the theory.]
criteria: [Do not silently add an eta equality absent from the chosen presentation.]

question: [Construct a function from $Pi_(x:A)Sigma_(y:B(x))R(x,y)$ to $Sigma_(f:Pi_(x:A)B(x))Pi_(x:A)R(x,f x)$. Explain why this does not introduce classical choice.]
hint1: [Each input already provides a pair at every $x$.]
hint2: [Define $f$ by first projection and its evidence by second projection.]
solution: [For input $h$, let $f=lambda x.pi_1(h x)$ and $r=lambda x.pi_2(h x)$. The second projection has type $R(x,pi_1(h x))$, which converts to $R(x,f x)$ by the beta rule for $f$. Hence $(f,r)$ has the target Sigma type. The premise is a function returning witness-and-proof pairs, not a mere truncated or classical assertion of existence; the construction reorganizes data already supplied.]
criteria: [Verify conversion of the dependent result and explain what the premise contains.]

question: [Construct maps between $Pi_(p:Sigma_(x:A)B(x))C(pi_1(p),pi_2(p))$ and $Pi_(x:A)Pi_(y:B(x))C(x,y)$. Verify their computation on pair inputs.]
hint1: [Evaluate an uncurried function on a constructed pair.]
hint2: [For the reverse, eliminate the input pair.]
solution: [Send $h$ to $lambda x.lambda y.h(x,y)$. Conversely send $k$ to the function defined on $(x,y)$ by $k x y$. Starting from $h$, the round trip at $(x,y)$ computes to $h(x,y)$; starting from $k$, the other round trip applied to $x,y$ computes to $k x y$. These pointwise equations follow from Pi and Sigma beta rules. An internal equality of the functions is not being inferred without function extensionality.]
criteria: [Check the dependent codomain in each direction and limit the equality claim.]

question: [Explain why exchanging $x:A,y:B(x)$ into $y:B(x),x:A$ is generally invalid, although weakening by a fresh declaration is often admissible. Give a concrete family example.]
hint1: [A context must be well formed from left to right.]
hint2: [Use $n:"Nat",v:"Vec"(D,n)$.]
solution:
[*Finding the approach.* A context is a sequence of well-formed judgments. Check the type of each declaration using only the prefix that precedes it.

*Argument.* For fixed $D:U_0$, consider $n:"Nat",v:"Vec"(D,n)$. The declaration of $v$ requires the previously available $n$ to form its type. Placing $v:"Vec"(D,n)$ first leaves $n$ unbound, so the context is not well formed. A fresh independent declaration can instead be inserted where all declarations remain well formed, and terms may be weakened accordingly. Exchange is admissible only when the dependency conditions permit it, unlike arbitrary exchange in a simple-type context.

In the valid prefix $D:U_0,n:"Nat"$, the expression $"Vec"(D,n)$ forms a type, so the next declaration is legal. After the proposed exchange, the prefix contains D but not n; formation of the vector type cannot even begin. By contrast a fresh declaration $z:C$ with C formed in the existing prefix may be appended, and old judgments can be weakened to the longer context. Inserting it earlier requires checking the types of all later declarations, not merely freshness of its name.

*A tempting dead end.* Freshness avoids name capture but does not guarantee that a declaration's type is available. A dependent exchange rule cannot be copied from the simply typed context rules unchanged.

*Hypotheses.* The vector family has an actual length parameter. Exchange remains permissible for declarations independent of each other, so the example rejects arbitrary exchange rather than all exchange.]
criteria: [Identify a formation failure, not merely an unconventional order.]
idea: [Validate each declaration against its preceding context; dependency order is part of the judgment.]

question: [For types $A$, $B(x)$, and $C(x,y)$, construct maps between $S=Sigma_(x:A)Sigma_(y:B(x))C(x,y)$ and $T=Sigma_(p:Sigma_(x:A)B(x))C("fst"(p),"snd"(p))$. Check all projection types and compute both composites on constructor inputs.]
hint1: [Both records store the same three pieces of data, grouped differently.]
hint2: [Track the third component's type after each projection; do not replace it by a constant type.]
solution:
[*Finding the approach.* The first two fields jointly determine the third field's type. Reassociation is therefore a typing calculation as well as a rearrangement of brackets.

*Argument.* Given $s:S$, put $a="fst"(s):A$, $q="snd"(s):Sigma_(y:B(a))C(a,y)$, $b="fst"(q):B(a)$, and $c'="snd"(q):C(a,b)$. Send s to $((a,b),c'):T$, since the projections of $(a,b)$ compute to a and b. Conversely, for $t:T$, put $p="fst"(t):Sigma_(x:A)B(x)$ and $c'="snd"(t):C("fst"(p),"snd"(p))$. Send it to $("fst"(p),("snd"(p),c')):S$. On $s=(a,(b,c'))$ the two maps produce $((a,b),c')$ and return the original constructor; on $t=((a,b),c')$ the reverse composite likewise returns t by projection computation.

*A tempting dead end.* An untyped tuple rearrangement hides whether the final proof inhabits the required fiber. Claiming a judgmental equality of these composites on arbitrary variable records would additionally require an eta principle not stipulated here.

*Hypotheses.* The families have the displayed dependencies and use the core Sigma formation, introduction, and projection computation rules. The claimed computation is on constructors.]
criteria: [List every projection's type and calculate both composites without assuming an unprovided eta rule.]
idea: [Reassociate the package while retaining the dependencies of later fields on earlier projections.]

question: [With addition recursive in its first argument, compute $"add"("suc"("zero"),n)$.]
hint1: [Use successor, then zero computation.]
hint2: [Keep the variable $n$ untouched.]
solution: [It reduces to $"suc"("add"("zero",n))$, then to $"suc"(n)$. No inspection of $n$ is necessary.]
criteria: [Show both computation steps.]

question: [State the motive for proving right-zero addition.]
hint1: [The statement must vary with the induction input.]
hint2: [Use an identity type indexed by $n$.]
solution: [The motive is $P(n)="Id"_"Nat"("add"(n,"zero"),n)$. At zero it reduces to reflexive equality; at successor the induction hypothesis can be lifted by congruence of successor.]
criteria: [State a family of types rather than a single fixed goal.]

question: [For $p:"Id"_A(a,b)$ and $u:B(a)$, state the type of $"transport"_B(p,u)$ and its reflexivity computation.]
hint1: [It moves evidence to the endpoint fiber.]
hint2: [At reflexivity the endpoints coincide.]
solution: [The result has type $B(b)$. When $p$ is $"refl"_a$, transport computes to $u:B(a)$.]
criteria: [Specify direction from $a$ to $b$.]

question: [If $A:U_1$ and $B(x):U_0$, find a universe containing $Pi_(x:A)B(x)$ and one containing $"Id"_A(a,b)$.]
hint1: [Use maximum for Pi and the base level for identity.]
hint2: [Both depend on the level of $A$.]
solution: [Both types belong to $U_1$: the Pi rule gives $max(1,0)=1$, and identity on a type in $U_1$ stays in $U_1$. No cumulativity is needed for these formation judgments.]
criteria: [Use the stated noncumulative conventions.]

question: [Prove addition associative by induction on its first argument.]
hint1: [Write the motive with the other two arguments fixed.]
hint2: [Lift the induction equality through successor.]
solution: [For fixed $n,k$, induct on $m$ with motive $"Id"("add"("add"(m,n),k),"add"(m,"add"(n,k)))$. At zero both sides compute to $"add"(n,k)$, so reflexivity suffices. At successor both sides compute to the successor of the respective sides for $m$. Apply congruence of successor to the induction hypothesis.]
criteria: [Reduce both sides before selecting the equality proof.]

question: [Describe and type both clauses of append on length-indexed vectors.]
hint1: [Recurse on the first vector, matching the recursion of addition.]
hint2: [The nil case length converts from $0+n$ to $n$.]
solution: [Append has type $"Vec"(A,m)->"Vec"(A,n)->"Vec"(A,"add"(m,n))$. At nil, return the second vector. At $"cons"(a,v)$, return $"cons"(a,"append"(v,w))$. The recursive result has length $"add"(m,n)$ for the tail length $m$, so the constructor has length $"suc"("add"(m,n))$, judgmentally equal to $"add"("suc"(m),n)$.]
criteria: [Check index conversion in both clauses.]

question: [Derive symmetry of identity with an explicit motive and reflexive case.]
hint1: [The desired output reverses endpoints.]
hint2: [Set $C(a,b,p)="Id"_A(b,a)$.]
solution: [Use the motive $C(a,b,p)="Id"_A(b,a)$. Path induction with this motive reduces the construction to $C(a,a,"refl"_a)="Id"_A(a,a)$. Supply $"refl"_a$. The eliminator then defines symmetry for every $p:"Id"_A(a,b)$ and computes to reflexivity on a reflexive input.]
criteria: [Allow the endpoint $b$ to vary in the motive.]

question: [For $f:A->D$, derive $"Id"_A(a,b)->"Id"_D(f(a),f(b))$. Why is this an implication about identity proofs rather than an equality-reflection rule?]
hint1: [Use path induction on the input proof.]
hint2: [The reflexive case is reflexivity at $f(a)$.]
solution: [Take motive $C(a,b,p)="Id"_D(f(a),f(b))$ and reflexive data $"refl"_(f(a))$. J supplies the function. Its result is a term of an identity type; it does not add the conversion judgment $f(a) equiv f(b)$ for an arbitrary variable $p$.]
criteria: [Distinguish an internal proof from a judgmental conversion.]

question: [Explain why a head function $"Vec"(A,"suc"(n))->A$ needs no nil branch. Can the same total signature be given for all lengths without extra data?]
hint1: [Constructor indices constrain which inputs can inhabit the domain.]
hint2: [Nil has length zero.]
solution: [Only a cons constructor can inhabit a successor-length vector in this inductive family, so head returns its first component. A function on all lengths would also have to handle nil; with arbitrary $A$ there may be no element to return, so such a uniform total head needs a nonempty-length condition, a default element, or an optional result type.]
criteria: [Use the index, not an unchecked runtime assumption.]

question: [For $p:"Id"_A(a,b)$ and $q:"Id"_A(b,c)$, prove transport along their composite agrees propositionally with successive transport on $u:B(a)$.]
hint1: [Induct on the paths, generalizing their endpoints appropriately.]
hint2: [After both become reflexivity, both expressions compute to $u$.]
solution: [Use path induction on $p$ and then $q$, with the target family asserting equality in $B(c)$ between $"transport"_B("trans"(p,q),u)$ and $"transport"_B(q,"transport"_B(p,u))$. Generalize the varying endpoints and retain $u$ in its proper starting fiber. At $p=q="refl"$, transitivity and both transports reduce, leaving $"Id"_(B(a))(u,u)$, inhabited by reflexivity. J lifts this base case to all endpoints and paths.]
criteria: [State the common result fiber and do not assume general paths compute.]

question: [Compare the left-zero and right-zero laws for addition. Explain why a proof of right-zero does not make its open expression reduce by definition.]
hint1: [Inspect which argument the recursive definition matches.]
hint2: [A variable in the first argument blocks computation.]
solution: [Left-zero $"add"("zero",n) equiv n$ follows directly by the defining equation. Right-zero for variable $n$ requires induction and produces a term of $"Id"("add"(n,"zero"),n)$. The recursive definition still cannot select a constructor of a variable, so the expression remains stuck under judgmental reduction. Equality elimination may transport along the proof, but equality reflection is not a rule of this theory.]
criteria: [Keep reduction, propositional proof, and transport distinct.]

question: [A student argues: “Apply J to $p:"Id"_A(a,a)$, so every such $p$ equals reflexivity.” Identify the missing motive issue; explain what J actually supplies.]
hint1: [J varies an endpoint before specializing to loops.]
hint2: [The alleged comparison to reflexivity is not well typed when the endpoint varies.]
solution:
[*Finding the approach.* Before applying J, type the proposed motive at a variable endpoint b. The flaw appears in that generic case, before the reflexivity case is considered.

*Argument.* In based path induction one must define a motive for arbitrary $b:A$ and $p:"Id"_A(a,b)$. The proposed equality between $p$ and $"refl"_a$ is not an identity type in one common fiber for arbitrary $b$, because reflexivity inhabits $"Id"_A(a,a)$ rather than $"Id"_A(a,b)$. Restricting the motive to $b=a$ before invoking J changes the eliminator. J permits valid families over all such endpoints, yielding transport and congruence; it does not by this argument yield the stronger K/UIP principle, which we have not assumed.

A valid based motive has a judgment $b:A,p:"Id"_A(a,b) tack.r C(b,p) "type"$. The tempting expression $"Id"_("Id"_A(a,b))(p,"refl"_a)$ fails because its second argument has type $"Id"_A(a,a)$ instead. Making b equal to a while checking this expression hides the formation problem; J requires a motive that was already defined at all endpoints. Valid motives, such as $B(a)->B(b)$, yield transport because their reflexive case is well typed.

*A tempting dead end.* One cannot replace a proof variable by reflexivity by fiat, or infer judgmental equality of endpoints from an identity proof. That would add principles absent from the specified theory.

*Hypotheses.* The core is intensional and does not assume K, UIP, or equality reflection. The failed proof diagnoses an invalid motive; it is not itself a proof of the metatheoretic independence of those principles.]
criteria: [Identify the exact ill-typed comparison rather than merely naming UIP.]
idea: [Check the motive's generic fiber first; an easy reflexivity case cannot repair an ill-formed family.]

objective: "U6 Transfer: A section respects changes of fiber"
question: [Let $B:A -> U$ and $f:Pi_(x:A)B(x)$. Given $p:"Id"_A(a,b)$, construct a term of $"Id"_(B(b))("transport"_B(p)(f(a)),f(b))$ and state its computation when $p$ is reflexivity. Explain why simply comparing $f(a)$ with $f(b)$ would not generally give a well-formed identity type.]
hint1: [Check the type of each endpoint of the proposed identity before trying to supply its proof.]
hint2: [Let the endpoint b and its equality p vary; when p is reflexivity, the transport disappears.]
solution:
[*Finding the approach.* Ordinary congruence works for a fixed codomain. Here the function's values lie in different fibers, so first move one value to the other's fiber. The resulting equality has a reflexive instance that can be extended over an arbitrary equality of inputs.

*Argument.* Fix a and form $C(b,p)="Id"_(B(b))("transport"_B(p)(f(a)),f(b))$ for arbitrary $b:A$ and $p:"Id"_A(a,b)$. The first endpoint is in $B(b)$ by the transport typing rule, and the second is in $B(b)$ by dependent application. Thus C is a valid motive. At $b=a,p="refl"_a$, the computation rule for transport reduces C to $"Id"_(B(a))(f(a),f(a))$, inhabited by $"refl"_(f(a))$. Based path induction J therefore yields a term in C(b,p) for every b and p. Its reflexive computation is exactly the chosen base term $"refl"_(f(a))$. Abstracting over a gives the assertion for all endpoints. Without transport, $f(a):B(a)$ and $f(b):B(b)$ need not have judgmentally equal types, so they cannot simply be placed into a homogeneous identity type.

*A tempting dead end.* Applying the ordinary congruence operation to f assumes a single fixed codomain. Replacing a by b informally throughout the context conceals the very transport whose compatibility is being proved. A propositional equality of inputs is not an equality-reflection rule.

*Hypotheses.* B and f are well-typed in the dependent theory, and transport is defined using J with its reflexive computation. The conclusion is an identity within one fiber, not a judgmental equality at arbitrary p. Neither function extensionality nor uniqueness of identity proofs is required.]
criteria: [Type both endpoints, give a motive at a general endpoint, and verify its reflexive case and computation.]
idea: [First align the fibers of the two function values, then extend the reflexive comparison over arbitrary equalities of inputs.]

question: [Describe a substitution from $Delta$ to the context $x:A,y:B(x)$.]
hint1: [Supply terms in declaration order.]
hint2: [The second term is checked after the first substitution.]
solution: [It consists of $a:A$ in $Delta$ and $b:B(a)$ in $Delta$. The second component cannot be checked in the uninstantiated family without accounting for $x:=a$.]
criteria: [State both component types in the source context.]

question: [Write the identity substitution on $x:A,y:B(x)$.]
hint1: [Use the context's own variables.]
hint2: [Check the dependent second component.]
solution: [It is the tuple $(x,y)$. The first component has type $A$ and the second type $B(x)$, so both match their declarations; applying it leaves terms and types unchanged.]
criteria: [Check the dependency as well as the names.]

question: [For $sigma:Delta->Gamma$ and $tau:Theta->Delta$, state the source and target of $sigma compose tau$ and the substitution equation for a term $t$ over $Gamma$.]
hint1: [Read composition right to left.]
hint2: [First reinterpret $t$ over $Delta$, then over $Theta$.]
solution: [The composite is $Theta->Gamma$ and $t[sigma][tau]=t[sigma compose tau]$. The rightmost substitution acts on the components supplied by the earlier one.]
criteria: [Do not reverse the order of context maps.]

question: [Contrast a canonical natural-number term with a neutral natural-number term.]
hint1: [Canonical forms expose a constructor.]
hint2: [A variable need not compute to a visible numeral in an open context.]
solution: [Zero and successor constructor forms are canonical introductions for naturals. A variable $n:"Nat"$ is neutral: no reduction selects whether it is zero or successor. In open reasoning it still has a valid type; “not a visible constructor” does not mean “ill typed.”]
criteria: [Separate canonical shape from typing validity.]

question: [Prove associativity of context-substitution composition from the term substitution law.]
hint1: [Compare the component corresponding to each declaration.]
hint2: [Both composites substitute twice into the same supplied term.]
solution: [Let $sigma:Delta->Gamma,tau:Theta->Delta,rho:Xi->Theta$. If the component of $sigma$ at a declaration of $Gamma$ is $s$, the component of $(sigma compose tau)compose rho$ is $s[tau][rho]$. The component of $sigma compose(tau compose rho)$ is $s[tau compose rho]$. The term substitution law equates these, with dependent types transported by the same law at each declaration. Thus the tuples agree componentwise.]
criteria: [Check component types, not just the first component's syntax.]

question: [For context extension $Gamma dot A$, verify $p compose chevron.l sigma,t chevron.r=sigma$ and $q[chevron.l sigma,t chevron.r]=t$ using tuple substitutions.]
hint1: [Pairing appends a last component.]
hint2: [Projection discards that last component; the generic variable selects it.]
solution: [The tuple $chevron.l sigma,t chevron.r$ lists the components of $sigma$ followed by $t$. Applying projection removes the final entry and leaves $sigma$. Substituting the tuple into the new last variable $q$ selects its last entry $t$. The type of this last entry is $A[sigma]$, as required.]
criteria: [Include the dependent type of the selected entry.]

question: [In the set interpretation, describe the meaning of a dependent sum for $A=\{0,1\}$, $B(0)=\{a\}$, $B(1)=\{b,c\}$. List its elements.]
hint1: [Keep tags identifying the starting fiber.]
hint2: [It is a disjoint union of fibers.]
solution: [The sum is $\{(0,a),(1,b),(1,c)\}$. The first projection records the index; the second projection is an element of the fiber determined by that first projection. Forgetting tags can conflate elements from different fibers in general.]
criteria: [List tagged pairs and connect them to dependent projection types.]

question: [For the same two fibers as #link(label("MM8036-U7.07"))[U7.07], list all dependent functions and count them.]
hint1: [Choose one value from each fiber.]
hint2: [The value at zero is forced; at one there are two choices.]
solution: [There are two functions: one with values $f(0)=a,f(1)=b$, the other with $g(0)=a,g(1)=c$. Each is a section assigning an element of the appropriate fiber. The count is $1 dot 2=2$, not the sum of fiber sizes.]
criteria: [A dependent function makes a simultaneous choice in every fiber.]

question: [Explain why interpreting $t[sigma]$ agrees with evaluating the interpretation of $t$ in the environment determined by $sigma$. Prove the variable and application cases.]
hint1: [Substitution and evaluation both proceed structurally.]
hint2: [For a variable, the tuple component is selected on either side.]
solution: [The variable case reads the corresponding component of the substitution environment, exactly the interpretation of that component term. For application $s u$, the induction hypotheses identify the interpretations of both substituted subterms with evaluation in the new environment; applying the interpreted function to the interpreted argument gives equality of the application interpretations. The abstraction case additionally extends the environment with the bound argument, which is why capture avoidance and lifted substitution matter.]
criteria: [Show the two required cases and identify the binder issue without omitting it from the general claim.]

question: [The set model interprets every identity proof between fixed endpoints, when one exists, by the same element. Explain why soundness alone does not prove syntactic UIP.]
hint1: [Soundness sends derivable equalities to semantic equalities.]
hint2: [Its implication points in only one direction.]
solution: [Soundness says a syntactic derivation has a valid interpretation. The interpretation may identify syntactically distinct proofs, because a model is allowed to forget distinctions. Deducing a syntactic UIP derivation from semantic identification would require an additional completeness or reflection theorem strong enough for that judgment. No such theorem has been established here, so the model's proof irrelevance cannot be imported as a rule of the paper theory.]
criteria: [State the direction of soundness and the missing converse.]

question: [Why does the equation $(t[sigma])[tau]=t[sigma compose tau]$ not by itself prove that an explicit-substitution rewrite system terminates? Construct a simple warning using orientations.]
hint1: [An equality can be oriented in either direction.]
hint2: [Allow both directions and a cycle appears.]
solution: [If both directions are permitted as reductions, the two expressions alternate forever whenever they are syntactically distinct. Even choosing one orientation for this equation does not settle interactions with all other rules. Termination requires a well-founded measure or another proof covering the actual oriented rule set. The typed equations in the lecture specify substitution behavior, not a termination theorem for every implementation of it.]
criteria: [Distinguish equational specification from an oriented operational system.]

question: [Let $A=\{0,1\}$ with fibers as in #link(label("MM8036-U7.07"))[U7.07], and let $sigma:\{r,s,t\}->A$ send $r,s$ to zero and $t$ to one. Describe the reindexed family, its total space, and its number of sections.]
hint1: [The fiber at an input is the old fiber at its image.]
hint2: [Two singleton fibers and one two-element fiber remain.]
solution:
[*Finding the approach.* Reindexing reads an existing family at new addresses. Keep the new address as a tag even when two addresses access the same old fiber.

*Argument.* The new fibers are $B(sigma(r))=\{a\}$, $B(sigma(s))=\{a\}$, and $B(sigma(t))=\{b,c\}$. The total space consists of $(r,a),(s,a),(t,b),(t,c)$, four tagged elements. A section must choose $a$ at both $r,s$ and choose either $b$ or $c$ at $t$, so there are two sections. This makes semantic substitution concrete: the index map changes where the fibers are read.

The entries at r and s both have value a, but $(r,a)$ and $(s,a)$ are distinct total-space elements because their first coordinates differ. A section must choose one value at every new address; it is not allowed to select only one point in the whole total space. The first two choices are forced and the last has two possibilities, giving the product $1 dot 1 dot 2=2$.

*A tempting dead end.* Collapsing equal fibers at r and s loses the base labels and changes the total space. Counting four total elements as four sections confuses one value with a complete assignment.

*Hypotheses.* The family and index map are the stated finite set data. These computations describe semantic objects and do not by themselves establish a syntactic derivability theorem.]
criteria: [Retain separate tags even when two fibers happen to be the same set.]
idea: [Retain the new base labels when reading old fibers, then count a section as one compatible choice per label.]

question: [Let $sigma:Delta->Gamma$ be a surjection of finite sets and let B be a family over Gamma. Characterize exactly which sections s of the reindexed family arise as $s=t compose sigma$ for a section t of B. Prove uniqueness and give an example of a section that does not arise this way.]
hint1: [Two addresses with the same image must receive the same value.]
hint2: [Use surjectivity for existence at each old address, and constancy on its fiber for independence of the chosen preimage.]
solution:
[*Finding the approach.* A reindexed section makes a choice at every new address. To recover a section at the old addresses, those choices must agree whenever the addresses refer to the same fiber.

*Argument.* The necessary and sufficient condition is $sigma(d)=sigma(d') => s(d)=s(d')$. Necessity follows at once from $s(d)=t(sigma(d))$. For sufficiency, at $g in Gamma$ take any d with $sigma(d)=g$ and define $t(g)=s(d)$, which belongs to $B(g)$. Surjectivity supplies such a d and the condition makes its value independent of the choice. Thus t is a section and pulls back to s. Any other t' has $t'(g)=s(d)=t(g)$ at every g, proving uniqueness. For a counterexample take Gamma a singleton, Delta two points r,s, and its sole fiber $\{0,1\}$. A reindexed section choosing zero at r and one at s is valid but cannot be pulled back from one choice at the singleton.

*A tempting dead end.* Surjectivity alone does not make arbitrary local choices compatible. It supplies preimages, not agreement of their values.

*Hypotheses.* The comparison concerns sections in the set model. The finite-set formulation avoids a need for an arbitrary family of choices, and the descended value is uniquely specified anyway.]
criteria: [Prove necessity, well-definedness, typing in the old fiber, uniqueness, and failure in the counterexample.]
idea: [Descent means constancy along the fibers of the index map, not just existence of local data.]

question: [Explain how contexts and substitutions form a category, naming identities and composition.]
hint1: [Use the equations from Unit 7.]
hint2: [Objects are well-formed contexts; arrows supply their variables.]
solution: [A morphism $Delta->Gamma$ is a well-typed simultaneous substitution for the declarations of $Gamma$ by terms over $Delta$, modulo the chosen definitional equality. Identity lists the context variables; composition substitutes one tuple into another. The identity and associativity equations establish the category laws.]
criteria: [Include the equality convention for arrows.]
